2.11. Having arranged everything carefully, on the next day he made the journey by carriage, but ordered Callirhoe—for he did not yet wish to show her to many—to be conveyed about evening by boat as far as the house, which was on the very harbor called Docimus; and he put the care of her in Plangon's hands.
2.12. So Callirhoe, when she was about to leave the country, first prayed to Aphrodite, and entering the temple and putting everyone out, said this to the goddess: "Mistress Aphrodite, am I to blame you justly, or to thank you? You joined me, a maiden, to Chaereas, and now after him you lead me as a bride to another.
2.13. I would not have been persuaded to swear by you and your son, had not this infant betrayed me," and she showed her belly. "I beseech you," she said, "not on my own behalf, but on his. Grant that my device may go unnoticed. Since he does not have his true father, let him pass for a child of Dionysius;
2.14. for when he is grown he will find that other father too." As she walked from the precinct to the sea, the sailors were seized with dread when they saw her, as though Aphrodite herself were coming to embark, and they rushed all together to worship her; and by the eagerness of the rowers the ship sailed into the harbor faster than words could tell. And at dawn the whole city was garlanded.
2.15. Each man sacrificed before his own house, and not in the temples alone. There was much talk as to who the bride was; and the more common sort of the multitude were persuaded, because of her beauty and because the woman was unknown, that a Nereid had come up from the sea, or that a goddess was present from the estates of Dionysius;
2.16. for this is what the sailors said. There was one desire in all, to behold Callirhoe, and the crowd gathered about the temple of Concord, where it was the custom for bridegrooms to receive their brides. Then for the first time since the tomb she adorned herself; for having once resolved to marry, she counted her beauty her country and her family. When she had put on Milesian dress and a bridal garland,

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.17. she looked out at the crowd. All then cried out, "Aphrodite is marrying!" They spread purple cloths beneath her, and roses and violets, and sprinkled perfume as she walked; not a child or an old man was left in the houses, nor even in the very harbors; the crowd, crowded for room, went up even onto the rooftops. But on this day too that malicious spirit again brought his envious displeasure; how, I will tell a little later. But first I wish to relate what happened in Syracuse at the same time.
3.1. The tomb-robbers had closed up the tomb carelessly, in their haste during the night; and Chaereas, watching for the very break of dawn, came to the tomb on the pretext of bringing garlands and libations, but in truth intending to make away with himself; for he could not endure to be parted from Callirhoe, and thought death the only physician of his grief. Coming there, he found the stones moved and the entrance plain to see.
3.2. Seeing this, he was astounded and held fast by a terrible perplexity over what had happened; and a swift rumor announced the strange thing to the Syracusans. So all ran together to the tomb, but no one dared to go inside before Hermocrates ordered it.
3.3. The man sent in reported everything exactly. It seemed incredible that not even the corpse was lying there. Then Chaereas himself asked, out of a longing to see Callirhoe again even dead; but searching the tomb he could find nothing.
3.4. Many went in after him out of disbelief; and helplessness seized them all, and one, standing there, said, "The grave-offerings have been plundered—the work of tomb-robbers; but where is the corpse?" Many and various reports held the crowd. And Chaereas, looking up to heaven and stretching out his hands, said, "Which of the gods, then, has become my rival and carried off Callirhoe, and now keeps her with him against her will, but forced by a stronger destiny?
3.5. For this reason she died suddenly too, that she might not understand. So Dionysus took Ariadne from Theseus, and Zeus took Semele. For I did not know that I had a goddess for a wife and that she was greater than belongs to our station. But she ought not to have departed from among men so quickly, nor on such a pretext.
3.6. Thetis was a goddess, yet she remained with Peleus, and he had a son by her; but I have been abandoned at the very height of love. What is to become of me? What shall I do, unfortunate? Shall I make away with myself? And with whom shall I be buried? For this was my one hope in my calamity: if I have not kept a common chamber with Callirhoe, I shall find a common tomb with her.
3.7. I make my defense to you, mistress, for my own life. You compel me to live; for I will seek you over land and sea, and, if I can, climb up into the very air. This I beg of you, my wife: do not flee from me." At this the crowd broke into lamentation, and all began to mourn for Callirhoe as for one just dead.
3.8. Triremes were at once launched, and many divided the search among them; for Hermocrates himself searched Sicily, and Chaereas Libya; some were sent off to Italy, and others were ordered to cross the Ionian Sea. But human help was altogether weak, and fortune brought the truth to light, without which no work is complete; and one may learn this from what happened.
3.9. For the tomb-robbers, having sold their cargo that was hard to dispose of, the woman, left Miletus and made their voyage toward Crete, hearing it was a prosperous and large island, on which they hoped the sale of their goods would be easy.

title: Callirhoe
text:
3.10. But a violent wind, taking them, drove them off into the Ionian Sea, and there they wandered on a deserted sea. Thunder and lightning and a long night fell upon the impious men, providence showing that before, for Callirhoe's sake, they had sailed prosperously. Each time they came near death, the god did not quickly release them from fear,
3.11. making the shipwreck long for them. So the land would not receive the impious men, and being at sea a long time they came to be in want of necessities, especially of drink, and their unjust wealth did them no good, but they were dying of thirst amid gold. Slowly, then, they repented of what they had dared, when it was no use, blaming one another.
3.12. So all the rest were dying of thirst, but Theron even at that time was a scoundrel; for stealing some of the drink, he robbed his fellow-robbers too. He thought he had done something clever, but it was really the work of providence, keeping the man for torture and the cross.
3.13. For the trireme carrying Chaereas fell in with the drifting cutter, and at first sheered off from it as from a pirate ship. But when it appeared to be without a helmsman, carried at random against the blows of the waves, one of the men on the trireme cried out, "It has no crew aboard; let us not be afraid, but go near and examine the strange thing."
3.14. This pleased the helmsman; for Chaereas was weeping in the hold of the ship, his face covered. When they came near, at first they called to those inside; but when no one answered, one went up from the trireme and saw nothing but gold and corpses. He reported it to the sailors; they rejoiced, thinking themselves fortunate, as having found a treasure at sea.
3.15. When there was an uproar, Chaereas asked the reason. Learning of it, he too wished to behold the strange sight. Recognizing the grave-offerings, he tore his clothes and cried out loud and far-resounding, "Alas, Callirhoe! These are yours. This garland is the one I placed on you; this your father gave you, this your mother; this is your bridal dress. The ship has become your tomb.
3.16. But your things I see; where are you? Only the corpse is missing from the grave-offerings." Hearing this, Theron lay like the corpses, for he was half-dead. He deliberated much whether to utter no sound at all or to move; for what was to come was not unforeseen by him; but man is by nature fond of life, and even in the uttermost calamities does not despair of a change for the better, the god who created us having sown this device in all, so that they should not flee a wretched life.
3.17. Held fast, then, by thirst, this was the first sound he uttered: "Drink." When it was brought to him and he received every care, Chaereas, sitting beside him, asked, "Who are you? Where are you sailing? Where did these things come from? And what have you done with their mistress?" Theron, scoundrel that he was, kept his wits about him and said, "I am a Cretan, sailing to Ionia;
3.18. I am seeking a brother of mine who is in the army. I was left behind by those on my ship in Cephallenia; and since their departure was sudden, I embarked from there on this cutter, which was sailing past at a good time. We were driven by extraordinary winds into this sea, then, when a long calm came on, all perished of thirst, and I alone was saved by my own piety." Hearing this, Chaereas ordered the cutter to be lashed to the trireme until they should sail into the harbors of Syracuse.
4.1. Rumor had gone ahead—being by nature swift, and at that time hastening the more to announce many things strange and new. So all ran together to the sea, and there were mingled feelings at once of weeping, wonder, inquiry, and disbelief; for the strange story astounded them.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.2. When the mother saw her daughter's grave-offerings, she wailed aloud, "I recognize everything; you alone, my child, are missing. O strange tomb-robbers, who kept the clothes and the gold but stole only my daughter!" The shores and harbors resounded with the women beating their breasts, and they filled land and sea with lamentation.
4.3. But Hermocrates, a general and a man experienced in affairs, said, "We must not seek here, but make a more lawful inquiry. Let us go to the assembly. Who knows whether there may be need of judges too?"
4.4. No sooner was the word spoken than the theater was full. The women too attended that assembly. The people sat in suspense, and Chaereas came in first, in black, pale, squalid, just as he had followed his wife to the tomb; and he would not go up onto the platform, but standing somewhere below, at first he wept for a long while and, wishing to speak, could not; and the crowd shouted, "Take courage and speak."
4.5. So at last, looking up, he said, "The present moment was not one for public speaking but for mourning; but I both speak and live by necessity, until I discover who took Callirhoe away. For this reason I sailed from here, and I do not know whether I have made the voyage fortunate or unfortunate.
4.6. For I saw a ship in fair weather drifting, full of its own storm and sinking in a calm. Wondering, we went near. I thought I was seeing the tomb of my poor wife, having all her things, except her. There was a multitude of corpses, but all strangers, and this one among them was found half-dead. This man I revived with every care and have kept for you."
4.7. Meanwhile public servants were leading Theron, bound, into the theater with a procession befitting him; for there followed him a wheel, a rack, fire, and whips, providence rendering him the prizes of his contests.
4.8. When he stood in the middle, one of the magistrates examined him. "Who are you?" "Demetrius." "Tell me, from where?" "A Cretan." "What do you know? Speak." "Sailing to Ionia to my brother, I was left behind by my ship, then embarked on a cutter that was sailing past. At the time I supposed they were merchants, but now tomb-robbers.
4.9. Being at sea a long time, all the rest perished for want of drink, and I alone was saved because I have done nothing wicked in my life. Do not you, then, men of Syracuse, a people famed for kindness, become to me wilder than thirst and the sea."
4.10. As he spoke piteously, pity came over the multitude, and he might soon have persuaded them, so as even to obtain provisions for his journey, had not some avenging spirit of Callirhoe begrudged him his unjust persuasion; for it was going to be the most monstrous of all things, that the Syracusans should be persuaded that the only one saved through impiety had been saved through piety—so that he might be the more punished.
4.11. Now there sat among the crowd a fisherman who recognized him and said quietly to those seated near him, "I saw this man before, prowling about our harbor." Quickly the word spread to more, and someone cried out, "He is lying." So the whole people turned about,
4.12. and the magistrates ordered the man who had first spoken to come down; and when Theron denied it, the fisherman was the more believed. They at once called for torturers, and whips were brought to the impious man; and though burned and cut, he held out a long while and almost overcame the tortures.
4.13. But great is each man's conscience, and the truth is all-powerful; for at last and slowly, but still, Theron confessed. He began, then, to tell his tale: "Seeing wealth being buried, I gathered robbers.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.14. We opened the tomb; we found the dead woman alive; we plundered everything and put it on the cutter; sailing to Miletus we sold only the woman, but the rest we were carrying to Crete; and being driven into the Ionian Sea by the winds, what we suffered you too have seen." Telling everything, he kept silent only about the name of the buyer.
4.15. When these things were said, joy and grief came over all—joy that Callirhoe lived, grief that she had been sold. So a vote of death was passed against Theron, but Chaereas begged that the man should not yet die, "so that," he said, "he may go and reveal to me the buyers. Consider my necessity: I am pleading for the man who sold my wife."
4.16. This Hermocrates prevented from happening, saying, "It is better to make the search more laborious than that the laws be undone. I beg you, men of Syracuse, remembering my generalship and my trophies, to repay me the favor in the matter of my daughter. Send an embassy on her behalf;
4.17. let us recover the free woman." While he was still speaking, the people cried out, "Let us all sail," and from the council the greater part volunteered. But Hermocrates said, "I thank you all for the honor, but two ambassadors from the people and two from the council are enough; and Chaereas shall sail as the fifth."
4.18. This was resolved and ratified, and on these terms he dissolved the assembly. As Theron was led away, a great part of the crowd followed. He was impaled before Callirhoe's tomb, and from the cross he looked upon that sea over which he had carried captive the daughter of Hermocrates, whom not even the Athenians had captured.
5.1. To all the rest it seemed best to wait for the season of sailing and to put out when spring shone forth; for it was still winter, and it seemed altogether impossible to cross the Ionian Sea. But Chaereas was in haste, ready, for love's sake, to yoke a raft and let himself be carried out to the open sea by the winds.
5.2. So the ambassadors too were unwilling to delay, out of respect both for him and especially for Hermocrates, and they prepared to sail. The Syracusans sent out the expedition at public expense, so that this too might add to the dignity of the embassy.
5.3. So they launched that admiral's trireme, which still had the tokens of victory. When the appointed day for putting out came, the multitude ran together to the harbor, not men only, but women and children too, and there were together prayers, tears, groans, comfort,
5.4. fear, courage, despair, hope. Ariston, the father of Chaereas, very old and worn out by sickness, clung to his son's neck and, hanging upon him, said weeping, "To whom do you leave me, my child, a half-dead old man? For that I shall see you no more is plain.
5.5. Wait even a few days, that I may die in your arms; bury me and then go." And his mother, taking hold of his knees, said, "I beg you, my child, do not leave me here desolate, but cast me into the trireme as a light burden; but if I am heavy and superfluous, throw me into the sea
5.6. over which you sail." Saying this she tore her breast and, holding out her breasts, said, "My child,
have respect for these and pity me,
me, if ever I held out to you the breast that lulls care.
Chaereas was broken down at his parents' entreaties and threw himself from the ship into the sea, wishing to die, that he might escape one of two things, either not seeking Callirhoe or grieving his parents; but the sailors quickly threw out and barely lifted him up.

title: Callirhoe
text:
5.7. Then Hermocrates dispersed the crowd and ordered the helmsman to put out at last. And something else happened too, a deed of friendship not ignoble. For Polycharmus, the companion of Chaereas, did not appear at the moment among them, but had said to his parents, "Chaereas is my friend—a friend indeed—yet not so far that I should share his uttermost dangers with him.
5.8. Therefore, until he sails off, I will keep out of the way." But when the ship had pushed off from land, he saluted them from the stern, so that they could no longer hold him back.
5.9. Going out of the harbor and looking out to the open sea, Chaereas said, "Bring me, sea, by the same course over which you brought Callirhoe. I pray you, Poseidon, either bring her too back with us, or do not bring me here without her. For if I cannot recover my wife, I wish at least to be a slave with her."
6.1. A favorable wind took the trireme, and it ran as though on the track of the cutter. In an equal number of days they came to Ionia and anchored on the same shore, in the estates of Dionysius.
6.2. So the rest, wearied, went ashore and hurried about their own refreshment, pitching tents and preparing a feast; but Chaereas, walking about with Polycharmus, said, "How can we now find Callirhoe? Above all I am afraid that Theron deceived us and that the poor woman is dead. But even if she has truly been sold, who knows where?
6.3. For Asia is large." Meanwhile, wandering, they came upon the temple of Aphrodite. It seemed good to them, then, to worship the goddess, and Chaereas, running to her knees, said, "You, mistress, first showed me Callirhoe at your festival; give her back to me now too, whom you granted me." And meanwhile, looking up, he saw beside the goddess a golden image of Callirhoe, a dedication of Dionysius.
And his knees and his heart gave way.
6.4. He fell down, dizzy with darkness; and the temple-keeper, seeing him, brought water, and reviving the man said, "Take courage, child; the goddess has astounded many others; for she is manifest and shows herself plainly. But this is a sign of some great good. Do you see the golden image? She was a slave, but Aphrodite has made her mistress of us all."
6.5. "And who is she?" said Chaereas. "The mistress of these estates, my child, the wife of Dionysius, the first of the Ionians." Hearing this, Polycharmus, being himself of sound mind, allowed Chaereas to say no more, but supporting him led him away from there, not wishing them to be discovered, who they were, before they had deliberated everything well and arranged it together.
6.6. Chaereas, while the temple-keeper was present, said nothing, but kept silent with self-control, except that his tears burst out of their own accord; and going far off, he threw himself alone upon the ground and said, "O kindly sea, why did you save me? Was it that, after a fair voyage, I should see Callirhoe the wife of another? I did not expect this ever to happen, not even if Chaereas were dead.
6.7. What shall I do, unhappy man? For I hoped to recover you from a master, and trusted that with the ransom I should persuade the buyer; but now I have found you wealthy, perhaps even a queen. How much more fortunate I would have been had I found you poor! Shall I go to Dionysius and say, 'Give me back my wife'? But who says that to a man who has married her?
6.8. And even if I meet you, I cannot come near you, nor even—the most common thing—greet you as a fellow-citizen. Perhaps I shall be in danger of perishing as the adulterer of my own wife." As he lamented thus, Polycharmus comforted him.

title: Callirhoe
text:
7.1. Meanwhile Phocas, the steward of Dionysius, having beheld a warship's trireme, was not without fear; and coaxing one of the sailors, he learned from him the truth—who they were, where from, and on whose account they sailed. He understood, then, that this trireme was bringing a great calamity to Dionysius, and that he would not live if Callirhoe were torn from him.
7.2. As one devoted to his master, wishing to forestall the danger and to quench a war great indeed, but not a public one, only of the house of Dionysius alone, for this reason he rode off to a fort of the barbarians and announced that an enemy trireme lay hidden, lurking perhaps for reconnaissance, perhaps for piracy, and that it was to the interest of the King's affairs that it should be seized before it did harm.
7.3. He persuaded the barbarians and brought them in formation. Falling upon the ship at midnight and casting in fire, they burned the trireme, and those they took alive they bound and led up to the fort. When the captives were divided, Chaereas and Polycharmus begged to be sold to one master. And the man who took them sold them into Caria. There, dragging heavy fetters, they worked on the estate of Mithridates.
7.4. To Callirhoe in a dream appeared Chaereas, bound and wishing to come to her, but unable; and she wailed loud and far-resounding in her sleep, "Chaereas, come here." Then for the first time Dionysius heard the name of Chaereas. When the woman was disturbed, he asked, "Who is it you were calling?" Her tears betrayed her, and she could not restrain her grief, but gave her feeling free rein.
7.5. "An unfortunate man," she said, "my husband from my maidenhood, not happy even in dreams; for I saw him bound. But you, poor man, have died seeking me—for your bonds signify your death—while I live and luxuriate, lying on a gilded couch with another man. Yet before long I shall come to you.
7.6. If even living we did not enjoy each other, dead we shall have each other." Hearing these words, Dionysius took various views: for jealousy laid hold of him, because she loved Chaereas even dead, and fear laid hold of him too, lest she should kill herself; yet he took courage, because the first husband seemed to the woman to be dead—for she would not, he thought, leave Dionysius, Chaereas being no longer alive.
7.7. He comforted the woman, then, as best he could, and for many days kept watch, lest she do herself some harm. But her grief was drawn off by the hope that perhaps he was alive and that her dream was false; and still more by her pregnancy; for in the seventh month after the wedding she bore a son, in appearance from Dionysius, but in truth from Chaereas. The city kept a very great festival, and embassies came from everywhere, the Milesians rejoicing with him that the line of Dionysius was increasing. And he, in his joy, yielded everything to his wife and proclaimed her mistress of the house. He filled the temples with dedications and feasted the whole city with sacrifices.
8.1. Callirhoe, anxious lest her secret be betrayed, asked that Plangon be set free—the only one who shared her secret, that she had come to Dionysius pregnant—so that she might have her loyalty secured not only by goodwill but by fortune too. "Gladly," said Dionysius, "do I reward Plangon for her service in love.
8.2. But we should do wrong if we honored the maidservant and did not render gratitude to Aphrodite, with whom we first saw each other." "I too," said Callirhoe, "wish this rather than you; for I owe her a greater gratitude. Now, then, I am still recovering from childbirth, but after waiting a few days we shall go more safely to the country."

title: Callirhoe
text:
8.3. She quickly recovered from the birth and became stronger and taller, no longer a girl, but having taken on the bloom of a woman. When they came to the country, Phocas prepared magnificent sacrifices; for a crowd had followed from the city. Beginning the hecatomb, Dionysius said, "Mistress Aphrodite, you are the cause of all my blessings.
8.4. From you I have Callirhoe, from you my son, and I am a husband and a father because of you. Callirhoe was enough for me, sweeter to me than country and parents, but I love the child because he has made the mother more securely mine. I have him as a pledge of her goodwill toward me. I beseech you, mistress, keep Callirhoe safe for me, and for Callirhoe
8.5. her son." The crowd standing around joined in the acclamation, and some with roses, some with violets, some with whole garlands strewed leaves upon them, so that the precinct was filled with flowers. Dionysius spoke his prayer in the hearing of all, but Callirhoe wished to speak to Aphrodite alone.
8.6. First she placed her son in her own arms, and there was seen a most beautiful sight, such as no painter has painted nor sculptor sculpted nor poet told of until now; for none of them has represented Artemis or Athena carrying an infant in her arms. Dionysius wept for pleasure as he looked, and quietly worshipped Nemesis; and ordering Plangon alone to remain, she sent the rest on ahead to the villa.
8.7. When they had gone, standing near Aphrodite and lifting the infant in her hands, she said, "For him, mistress, I acknowledge gratitude to you; for myself I do not know. Then I would have acknowledged gratitude for myself too, had you kept Chaereas for me. Yet you have given me an image of my dearest husband, and you have not taken Chaereas from me altogether.
8.8. Grant, then, that my son may become more fortunate than his parents and like his grandfather; may he too sail on an admiral's trireme, and may someone say, when he is fighting at sea, 'The grandson is greater than Hermocrates.' For his grandfather too will rejoice to have a successor of his valor, and we, his parents, shall rejoice even when dead.
8.9. I beseech you, mistress, be reconciled to me henceforth; for I have been unfortunate enough. I have died, I have come back to life, I have been robbed, I have fled, I have been sold, I have been a slave; and I count my second marriage still heavier than these. But one favor in return for all I ask of you, and through you of the other gods: keep my orphan safe." While she still wished to speak, her tears stopped her.
9.1. After a little while she called the priestess; and the old woman, answering, said, "Why do you weep, my child, in the midst of such blessings? For already strangers worship you as a goddess too. The other day two handsome young men came here, sailing past; and one of them, beholding your image, all but breathed his last. So manifest has Aphrodite made you."
9.2. This struck Callirhoe's heart, and as though gone mad, fixing her eyes, she cried out, "Who were the strangers? Where were they sailing from? What did they tell you?" The old woman, frightened, at first stood speechless, but at last said, "I only saw them; I heard nothing." "What did they look like?
9.3. Recall their appearance." The old woman described it, not exactly, but Callirhoe nevertheless suspected the truth; for what each person wishes, that he believes. Looking toward Plangon she said, "It is possible that the unhappy Chaereas, wandering, is here. What, then, has happened? Let us seek him, but in silence."

title: Callirhoe
text:
9.4. So coming to Dionysius she said only this, what she had heard from the priestess; for she knew that love is by nature curious, and that he would of his own accord inquire about what had happened. And so it came about. For Dionysius, on learning of it, was at once filled with jealousy, and was far from suspecting Chaereas, but feared that some adulterous plot was lurking about the country; for the beauty of his wife persuaded him to suspect everything and to fear.
9.5. And he feared not only plots from men, but expected too that perhaps a god might come down from heaven against him as a rival. So calling Phocas he questioned him closely: "Who are the young men and from where? Are they rich and handsome? And why did they worship my Aphrodite? Who told them of her?
9.6. Who allowed it?" But Phocas concealed the truth, not from fear of Dionysius, but knowing that Callirhoe would destroy both him and his family, if she learned of what had happened. So when he denied that any had come, Dionysius, not knowing the reason, suspected that some heavier plot was being set up against him.
9.7. Enraged, then, he demanded whips and the rack for Phocas, and called together not only him but all those on the estates, convinced that he was searching out adultery. Perceiving into what danger he had come, whether speaking or keeping silent, Phocas said, "To you, master,
9.8. I will tell the truth alone." So Dionysius sent everyone away and said, "See, we are alone. Lie no more; tell the truth, even if it is bad." "There is nothing bad, master," he said, "for I bring you tidings of great blessings; and if the first of them are gloomier, do not for that be at all anxious or grieved, but wait until you hear everything;
9.9. for it has a good ending." So Dionysius, raised to suspense by the announcement and hanging upon the hearing, said, "Do not delay, but tell it now." Then he began: "A trireme has sailed in here from Sicily, with ambassadors of the Syracusans demanding Callirhoe back from you."
9.10. Dionysius almost died when he heard it, and night poured over his eyes; for he took the impression that Chaereas was standing over him and tearing Callirhoe away. So he lay there, presenting the look and color of a corpse, and Phocas was in perplexity, unwilling to call anyone, lest there be a witness of the secrets; but slowly and little by little he himself revived his master, saying, "Take courage; Chaereas is dead; the ship is destroyed; there is no longer any fear." These words put life into Dionysius,
9.11. and little by little coming to himself again he inquired closely about everything, and Phocas told of the sailor who had informed him, where the trireme was from and on whose account they sailed and who were the men present, his own stratagem against the barbarians, the night, the fire, the shipwreck, the slaughter, the bonds. So, as a cloud or darkness was lifted from his soul, Dionysius embraced Phocas and said, "You are my benefactor, you a true guardian and most faithful in secrets.
9.12. Through you I have Callirhoe and my son. I would not have ordered you to kill Chaereas, but since you have done it I do not blame you; for the wrong was done out of love for your master. This one thing only you did carelessly: you did not inquire whether Chaereas is among the dead or among the bound. You ought to have sought the corpse; for he too would have had a burial, and I would have had more secure assurance. But I cannot now enjoy my good fortune free from care, because of the bound men; for we do not even know this, where any of them has been sold."

title: Callirhoe
text:
10.1. Ordering Phocas to relate the rest of what had happened openly, but to keep silent on these two things, his own stratagem and that some of those from the trireme were still alive, Dionysius came to Callirhoe gloomy; then he gathered together the country people, primed beforehand, so that the woman, on learning what had happened, might now take a more settled despair concerning Chaereas.
10.2. So they came and told—and all knew it—that "barbarian pirates from somewhere, running down by night, burned a Greek trireme that had anchored the day before off the shore; and by day we saw water mingled with blood and
10.3. corpses carried by the waves." When the woman heard this, she tore her clothes, and beating her eyes and cheeks she ran up to the room into which she had first come when sold. Dionysius gave her grief free rein, fearing he might become tiresome if he were present at the wrong time. So he ordered all to depart, and Plangon alone to attend her, lest she do herself some harm.
10.4. Callirhoe, finding quiet, sat down on the ground, and pouring dust on her head and tearing her hair, began such laments as these: "I prayed to die before you or with you, Chaereas; but now it is at all events necessary for me to die after you; for what hope is still left to keep me in life?
10.5. Unfortunate until now, I used to reason, 'I shall see Chaereas one day and tell him how much I have suffered for his sake; this will make me dearer to him. With how much joy will he be filled when he sees his son!' All this has become useless to me, and the child too is now superfluous; for an orphan has been added to my misfortunes.
10.6. Unjust Aphrodite, you alone saw Chaereas, but did not show him to me when he came; you handed his beautiful body into the hands of pirates; you did not pity the man who sailed for your sake. To such a goddess who would pray—you who killed your own suppliant?
10.7. You did not help him on that fearful night, when you saw a handsome youth, a lover, murdered near you; you took from me my contemporary, my fellow-citizen, my lover, my beloved, my bridegroom.
10.8. Give me back at least his corpse. I grant that we were born the most unfortunate of all; but how did the trireme do wrong, that barbarians should burn it—the one not even the Athenians mastered? Now the parents of us both sit by the sea, awaiting our homecoming, and whenever any ship is seen far off, they say, 'Chaereas comes, bringing Callirhoe'; they make ready for us the bridal bed, and a chamber is adorned for those who have not even a tomb of their own. O foul sea, you both brought Chaereas to Miletus to be murdered and me to be sold!"
1.1. So Callirhoe spent that night in laments, mourning Chaereas while he was still alive; and dozing off for a little while she saw in a dream a band of barbarian pirates bringing fire, a trireme in flames, and herself running to help Chaereas.
1.2. Dionysius was grieved to see his wife wasting away, lest some of her beauty be lost to her, but he supposed it to be to the advantage of his own love that she should give up her former husband for good.
1.3. Wishing, then, to show affection and magnanimity, he said to her, "Rise, woman, and prepare a tomb for the poor man. Why do you strive after impossible things, but neglect what is necessary? Imagine him standing over you and saying, 'Bury me as quickly as may be, that I may pass the gates of Hades.' For even if the body of the unfortunate man has not been found, still this is an ancient custom of the Greeks, to honor with tombs even those who cannot be found."

title: Callirhoe
text:
1.4. He persuaded her quickly, for the advice was to her liking. So when occupation fell upon her, her grief abated, and rising from her bed she looked about for a place in which to make the tomb. It pleased her to have it near the temple of Aphrodite, so that those of later times too might have a memorial of her love.
1.5. But Dionysius grudged Chaereas the neighborhood and kept that place for himself. So, wishing at the same time to keep the occupation going longer, he said, "Let us go, woman, to the city, and there, before the city, let us build a high and conspicuous tomb, that it may be seen from afar by men out at sea. The harbors of Miletus are fine, and the Syracusans too often put in there. So among your fellow-citizens too your generosity will not lack renown."
1.6. This proposal pleased Callirhoe, and for the time she checked her haste; but when she came to the city, on a high beach she began to build a tomb, in everything like her own in Syracuse—the shape, the size, the costliness—and this one too, like that, for a living man. When, with lavish expense and many hands, the work was quickly finished, then at last she also imitated the funeral procession held over it.
1.7. For a fixed day was announced beforehand, and to it came not only the multitude of the Milesians but of nearly all Ionia. And two satraps too were present, who happened to be staying there at the time, Mithridates of Caria and Pharnaces of Lydia.
1.8. The pretext was to honor Dionysius, but the truth was to see Callirhoe. For the fame of the woman was great over all Asia, and the name of Callirhoe was rising even to the great King, such as not even that of Ariadne or Leda. But on that day she proved greater than her reputation; for she came forth in black, with her hair loosed; and flashing in her face and baring her arms she appeared more than the White-Armed and the Fair-Ankled of Homer.
1.9. Not one even of the others could endure the dazzling brightness of her beauty, but some turned away, as when a sunbeam falls upon them, and worshipped. Even children were affected. But Mithridates, the governor of Caria, fell down speechless, like a man struck unexpectedly by a sling-stone, and his attendants could barely support and carry him.
1.10. In the procession there was carried a portrait of Chaereas, fashioned after the seal on the ring; but although the image was very beautiful, no one looked at it while Callirhoe was present, but she alone won over the eyes of all.
1.11. How could anyone fittingly describe the close of the procession? For when they came near the tomb, those carrying the bier set it down, and Callirhoe, mounting upon it, threw herself upon Chaereas and, kissing the image, said, "You buried me first in Syracuse,
1.12. and I in turn bury you in Miletus. For our misfortunes are not only great but strange: we have buried each other. And neither of us even has the other's corpse. Envious Fortune, even in death you have grudged us to be laid in common earth, and you have made even our corpses exiles." The crowd broke into lamentation, and all pitied Chaereas, not because he was dead, but because he had been deprived of such a wife.
2.1. So Callirhoe was burying Chaereas in Miletus, while Chaereas in Caria was working in bonds. Digging the ground, he was quickly worn out; for many things weighed upon him—toil, neglect, his fetters, and more than these, his love. He wished to die, but a slender hope would not let him, that perhaps he might one day see Callirhoe.

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.2. So Polycharmus, his friend taken captive with him, seeing that Chaereas could not work but was receiving blows and being shamefully abused, said to the overseer of the work, "Mark off for us a portion of our own, so that you may not charge against us the idleness of the other prisoners; and we will render our own measure by
day." He was persuaded and granted it.
2.3. And Polycharmus, being a young man of manly nature and not enslaved to love, a harsh tyrant, worked the two portions almost by himself alone, gladly taking the larger share of the labor, in order to save his friend.
2.4. So these men were in such misfortunes, learning their loss of freedom late; but Mithridates the satrap returned to Caria not such as he had set out for Miletus, but pale and thin, as having a wound in his soul, warm and sweet.
2.5. Wasting away with love of Callirhoe, he would certainly have died, had he not met with some such consolation as this. Some of the laborers bound together with Chaereas—they were sixteen in number, shut up in a dark hut—broke through their fetters by night, cut the overseer's throat, and then attempted to flee.
2.6. But they did not escape, for the dogs on guard betrayed them. So, caught that night, they were all bound more carefully in the stocks, and by day the steward reported the affair to his master; and he, without even seeing them or hearing their defense, at once ordered the sixteen hut-mates to be crucified.
2.7. So they were led out bound together by the feet and necks, and each of them carried his own cross; for to the necessary punishment those who carried it out added the gloomy external spectacle, as an example of fear to others like them. Chaereas, as he was led off, kept silent, but Polycharmus, bearing his cross, said, "Because of you, Callirhoe, we suffer these things.
2.8. You are the cause to us of all our evils." When the steward heard these words, he thought there was some woman privy to what had been dared. So, that she too might be punished and an inquiry made into the plot, he quickly tore Polycharmus from the common chain and led him to Mithridates. He was lying in a garden, alone and idling, picturing to himself Callirhoe such as he had seen her in mourning; and being wholly absorbed in that thought, he looked on the servant with displeasure.
2.9. "Why do you disturb me?" he said. "It is necessary, master," he said; "for I have found the source of the great crime, and this accursed man knows of a foul woman who had a hand in the murder." Hearing this, Mithridates knit his brows and, with a terrible look, said, "Tell me
2.10. the woman who shared and was your accomplice in the crimes." But Polycharmus denied that he knew of any, since he had had no share at all in the deed. Whips were called for, and fire was brought, and there was a preparation of instruments of torture, and one, already laying hold of his body, said, "Tell the name of the woman whom you confessed to be the cause of your evils." Polycharmus said, "Callirhoe."
2.11. The name struck Mithridates, and he thought the woman must have some unlucky sameness of name with that other. So he no longer wished to press the examination eagerly, fearing lest he should ever come into the necessity of insulting that sweetest of names; but when his friends and servants urged a more exact inquiry,
2.12. he said, "Let Callirhoe be brought." So, beating Polycharmus, they asked who she was and from where they should bring her. The poor man, at a loss, was unwilling to lie about any woman, and said, "Why are you troubling yourselves in vain, seeking one who is not here? I was mentioning Callirhoe of Syracuse, the daughter

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.13. of Hermocrates the general." Hearing this, Mithridates was filled with blushing, and sweated inwardly, and somewhere a tear, against his will, fell from him, so that even Polycharmus fell silent and all present were at a loss. At last and with difficulty Mithridates, collecting himself, said, "What is your business with that Callirhoe, and why, when about to die, did you mention her?" He answered, "It is a long tale, master, and no longer of any use to me.
2.14. I will not trouble you by babbling out of season, and at the same time I am afraid that, if I delay, my friend may die before me; and I wish to die together with him." The anger of the hearers was broken, and their wrath turned to pity, and Mithridates, beyond all the rest, was overcome and said, "Do not be afraid, for you will not trouble me by telling it;
2.15. for I have a kindly soul. Tell everything boldly and leave out nothing—who you are and from where, and how you came to Caria, and why you dig in bonds; and above all tell me about Callirhoe, and who your friend is."
3.1. So Polycharmus began to speak: "We two prisoners are Syracusans by birth. But the one is a young man once the first in Sicily for renown and wealth and beauty, while I am of humble station, but his schoolfellow and friend.
3.2. Leaving our parents, we sailed from our country, I for his sake, he for the sake of a woman named Callirhoe, whom, thinking her dead, he had buried at great cost; but tomb-robbers, finding her alive, sold her into Ionia. This Theron the pirate revealed to us, being publicly tortured.
3.3. So the city of the Syracusans sent a trireme and ambassadors to seek out the woman. This trireme, lying at anchor by night, the barbarians burned, and they slaughtered the many, but bound and sold here me and my friend. We then bore the calamity soberly; but certain others bound together with us, whom we do not know, broke their fetters and committed murder, and at your command we were all led to the cross.
3.4. So my friend, even in dying, made no complaint against the woman, but I was led to mention her and to say that she was the cause of our evils, on whose account we sailed." While he was still speaking, Mithridates cried out, "You mean Chaereas."
3.5. "My friend," said Polycharmus; "but I beg you, master, order the executioner not even to part our crosses." Tears and groaning followed the tale, and Mithridates sent everyone to Chaereas, so that he should not die first. They found the others already executed, and him just mounting the cross.
3.6. So from afar they cried out, one one thing and one another: "Spare him! Come down! Do not wound him! Let him go!" The executioner checked his hand, and Chaereas, grieved, came down from the cross; for he was glad to be quit of a wretched life and an unhappy love. As he was led off, Mithridates met him and, embracing him, said, "Brother and friend, you almost trapped me into doing an impious deed, through your controlled but ill-timed silence."
3.7. At once, then, he ordered his servants to take them to the baths and tend their bodies, and when they had bathed, to put on them costly Greek cloaks; and he himself invited acquaintances to a banquet and sacrificed a thank-offering for Chaereas's deliverance. The drinking was long and the entertainment pleasant, and nothing of cheer was lacking.
3.8. As the feast went on, Mithridates, warmed with wine and love, said, "It is not your bonds and your cross that I pity, Chaereas, but that you have been deprived of such a wife." Astonished, Chaereas cried out, "Where, then, did you see my Callirhoe?" "No longer yours," said Mithridates, "but lawfully married to Dionysius of Miletus; and now

title: Callirhoe
text:
3.9. they even have a child." Chaereas could not endure to hear this, but falling at the knees of Mithridates said, "I beseech you, master, give me back my cross. You torture me worse, compelling me to live after such a tale.
3.10. Faithless Callirhoe, most impious of all women, I was sold for your sake, and dug, and bore a cross, and was handed to the executioner's hands, while you luxuriated and celebrated a wedding while I was in bonds. It was not enough that you became another man's wife while Chaereas lived;
3.11. you have become a mother too." All began to weep, and the banquet turned to a gloomy theme. Alone of them Mithridates rejoiced at this, taking a certain amorous hope, as being now able both to say and to do something about Callirhoe,
3.12. so that he might seem to be helping a friend. "For now," he said, "since it is night, let us go away, and on the next day, when sober, let us deliberate about these things; for the matter needs longer leisure." On this he rose and dissolved the banquet, and he himself rested, as was his custom, but for the young Syracusans he appointed attendance and a special chamber.
4.1. That night, full of cares, came upon all, and no one could sleep; for Chaereas was angry, Polycharmus comforted him, and Mithridates rejoiced, hoping that, just as in the athletic contests, being the reserve competitor between Chaereas and Dionysius, he himself would carry off the prize, Callirhoe, without a struggle.
4.2. On the next day, when the question was put forward, Chaereas at once thought it best to go to Miletus and demand his wife from Dionysius; for, he said, Callirhoe would not remain when she saw him. But Mithridates said, "For my part, go, for I do not wish you to be parted from your wife a single day; would that you had never left Sicily, and that nothing dreadful had befallen you both. But since fortune, fond of novelty, has wrapped a gloomy drama about you, you must deliberate about what follows more prudently; for now you are hurrying out of passion rather than reason, foreseeing nothing of the future.
4.3. Alone and a stranger, you are going off to the greatest city, and you wish to take away from a wealthy man, the foremost in Ionia, a wife especially bound to him—relying on what power? Far off are Hermocrates and Mithridates, your only allies, able rather to mourn you than to help you.
4.4. I fear too the fortune of the place. You have already suffered dreadful things there; but your past will seem to you kinder.
You were bound, but you lived; you were sold, but to me. Now, if Dionysius perceives you plotting against his marriage, what god will be able to save you? You will be handed over to a rival who is a tyrant, and perhaps you will not even be believed to be Chaereas; and you will be in still greater danger if he does think you are truly he.
4.5. Are you alone ignorant of the nature of love, that this god delights in deceptions and tricks? It seems to me best for you first to make trial of the woman by letter, whether she remembers you and wishes to leave Dionysius, or
wishes to increase the house of him who has married her.
4.6. Write her a letter; let her grieve, rejoice, seek, summon; and for the sending of the letter I will provide. Go and write." Chaereas was persuaded, and going off into solitude wished to write, but could not, his tears flowing and his hand trembling. Having wept out his own misfortunes, he barely began such a letter as this:
CHAEREAS TO CALLIRHOE
4.7. I am alive, and I am alive because of Mithridates, my benefactor, and, I hope, yours too. For I was sold into Caria by the barbarians who burned the beautiful trireme, the admiral's ship, your father's; and on it the city sent an embassy on your behalf. What has become of the other citizens I do not know, but me and Polycharmus my friend, when we were already about to be killed, the pity of a master saved.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.8. But while Mithridates has done me every kindness, in this one thing he has grieved me beyond all: that he told me of your marriage. For death, being a man, I expected, but your marriage I did not look for. Yet I beseech you, change your mind. Over these letters of mine I pour out tears and kisses.
4.9. I am that Chaereas of yours, whom you saw as a maiden walking to Aphrodite's temple, for whom you lay sleepless. Remember the bridal chamber and the mystic night, in which you first took experience of a husband and I of a wife. But I was jealous. This is the way of a lover. I have paid the penalty to you.
4.10. I was sold, I was a slave, I was bound. Do not bear me a grudge for that rash kick; for I too mounted a cross for your sake, bringing no charge against you. If, then, you still remember me, I have suffered nothing; but if you think otherwise, you will be passing on me a sentence of death.
5.1. This letter he gave to Hyginus, his most trusted man, whom he had as steward of his whole estate in Caria, having disclosed to him his own love as well. He himself also wrote to Callirhoe, showing goodwill and care toward her, that for her sake he had saved Chaereas, and advising her not to outrage her first husband, promising that he himself would manage matters so that they should recover each other, if she too added her vote.
5.2. He sent with Hyginus three attendants and costly gifts and abundant gold; and it was given out to the other servants that he was sending these to Dionysius, so as to avert suspicion. He ordered Hyginus, when he came to Priene, to leave the others there, and to go himself alone, as an Ionian—for he spoke Greek—as a scout into Miletus; and then, when he had learned how he might deal with the business, to bring those from Priene to Miletus.
5.3. So he went off and did as he was ordered, but fortune awarded an end not like the plan, but set in motion the beginning of greater events. For when Hyginus had gone off to Miletus, the slaves, left behind, free of their overseer, rushed into dissipation, having gold in abundance.
5.4. In a small city, full of Greek inquisitiveness, foreign extravagance turned the eyes of all upon them; for being unknown men and living luxuriously they seemed to them most likely pirates, and at all events runaways.
5.5. So the magistrate came to the inn and, searching, found gold and costly ornaments; and thinking them stolen, he examined the servants as to who they were and where these things came from. Out of fear of torture they revealed the truth, that Mithridates the governor of Caria had sent gifts to Dionysius,
5.6. and they showed the letters. But the magistrate did not open the writings, for they were sealed on the outside; instead, handing everything over to public officers along with the servants, he sent them to Dionysius, thinking to lay up a benefit toward him.
5.7. Now it happened that Dionysius was entertaining the most distinguished of the citizens, and the banquet was brilliant, and already somewhere a flute was sounding and a melody was heard in song. In the midst of it someone handed him the letter:
BIAS, MAGISTRATE OF PRIENE, TO HIS BENEFACTOR DIONYSIUS, GREETING
5.8. Gifts and letters being conveyed to you from Mithridates the governor of Caria, wicked slaves were squandering, whom I have arrested and sent up to you.
This letter Dionysius read in the midst of the banquet, preening himself on the royal gifts; and ordering the seals to be cut, he tried to read the writings. So he saw:

title: Callirhoe
text:
CHAEREAS TO CALLIRHOE. I am alive.
5.9. And his knees and his heart gave way, and then darkness poured over his eyes. And yet, though fainting, he kept hold of the letters, fearing that another might read them. When there was an uproar and a running together, he was roused, and understanding his condition he ordered the servants to carry him into another room, as though wishing to take some rest.
5.10. So the banquet broke up gloomily—for an impression of a stroke had seized them—but Dionysius, alone by himself, read the letters over many times. Various feelings laid hold of him—anger, despondency, fear, disbelief. He did not believe that Chaereas was alive—for this he did not at all wish—but supposed it an adulterous pretense of Mithridates, who wished to corrupt Callirhoe by the hope of Chaereas.
6.1. So on the next day he set a stricter watch over the woman, lest anyone approach her or report any of the tales from Caria; and he himself devised such a defense as this. There was staying there at the time the governor of Lydia and Ionia, Pharnaces, who indeed seems the greatest of those sent down by the King to the sea. To him Dionysius went, for he was his friend, and asked for a private interview. "I beseech you, master," he said, "help both me and yourself. For Mithridates, the worst of men, who envies you too, having become my guest-friend, is plotting against my marriage and has sent adulterous letters with gold to
6.2. my wife." On this he read the letters and told of the trick. Pharnaces heard his words gladly—perhaps partly because of Mithridates (for there had been no few collisions between them on account of their neighborhood), but more because of love; for he too was burning for Callirhoe and on her account stayed much in Miletus, inviting Dionysius with his wife to his banquets.
6.3. He promised, then, to help him as far as he could, and wrote a secret letter:
TO THE KING OF KINGS, ARTAXERXES, PHARNACES, SATRAP OF LYDIA AND IONIA, TO HIS OWN MASTER, GREETING.
6.4. Dionysius of Miletus is your slave, from his ancestors faithful and zealous toward your house. He has complained to me that Mithridates the governor of Caria, having become his guest-friend, is corrupting his wife. This brings great discredit on your affairs, or rather disturbance. For every lawlessness of a satrap is blameworthy, but most of all this. For Dionysius is the most powerful of the Ionians, and the beauty of the woman is famous, so that the outrage cannot be hidden.
6.5. This letter, when it was brought, the King read to his friends and deliberated about what should be done. Various opinions were spoken; for those who envied Mithridates, or coveted his satrapy, thought it best not to overlook a plot against the marriage of a man of repute, while those of more easygoing natures, or who honored Mithridates—and he had many supporters in high places—were not pleased to seize an esteemed man on a slander.
6.6. As the opinions were divided, the King ratified nothing on that day, but deferred the consideration; but when night came on, there crept over him a hatred of wrongdoing for the sake of the dignity of the kingship, and a caution about the future; for Mithridates, he thought, would have a beginning of contempt for authority.
6.7. So he set out to summon him to trial; but another feeling urged him to send for the beautiful woman as well. His counselors, and the darkness that comes in solitude, reminded the King of this part of the letter too; and rumor too provoked him, that there was a certain Callirhoe, most beautiful, in Ionia. And this only the King blamed Pharnaces for, that he had not added in the letter the name of the woman.

title: Callirhoe
text:
6.8. Yet, on the uncertain chance that the other might prove even better than the one reported, he resolved to summon the woman too. So he wrote to Pharnaces:
Send up Dionysius, my slave, the Milesian.
And to Mithridates:
Come and make your defense, that you did not plot against the marriage of Dionysius.
7.1. Mithridates was astounded and at a loss as to the reason for the slander, when Hyginus, returning, made clear what had happened concerning the servants. Betrayed, then, by the letters, he deliberated whether not to go up, fearing the slanders and the King's wrath, but to seize Miletus and destroy Dionysius the cause, and, snatching up Callirhoe, to revolt from the King.
7.2. "Why are you in haste," he said, "to surrender your freedom into a master's hands? Perhaps you will even prevail by remaining here; for the King is far off and has his generals; and even if otherwise he should set you aside, you will be able to suffer nothing worse. Meanwhile do not betray two of the fairest things, love and dominion. Sovereignty is a glorious shroud, and with Callirhoe death is sweet."
7.3. While he was still deliberating thus and preparing for revolt, someone came announcing that Dionysius had set out from Miletus and was bringing Callirhoe with him. This Mithridates heard with more grief than the order summoning him to trial; and weeping out his own misfortune he said, "On what hopes do I still remain?
7.4. Fortune betrays me on every side. Perhaps the King will pity me, since I do no wrong; but if I must die, again I shall see Callirhoe; and at the trial I shall have Chaereas with me, and Polycharmus, not only as advocates but as witnesses." So, ordering all his retinue to follow, he set out from Caria, with a good heart from the appearance of doing no wrong; so that they did not even escort him with tears, but with sacrifices and a procession.
7.5. So Love sent forth this one expedition from Caria, but from Ionia another more glorious; for the beauty was more conspicuous and more royal. For the woman's fame ran ahead, announcing to all men that Callirhoe was coming, the famous name, the great masterpiece of nature,
like Artemis or golden Aphrodite.
7.6. The story of the trial too made her more renowned. Whole cities came to meet her, and those who ran together to the sight crowded the roads; and to all the woman seemed greater than her fame. But Dionysius, though counted blessed, was grieved, and the magnitude of his good fortune made him more fearful; for, being an educated man, he reflected that Love is fond of novelty; for this reason poets and sculptors have given him bow and fire,
7.7. the lightest things and unwilling to stand still. And the memory of old tales came over him, how many changes there have been among beautiful women. Everything, then, frightened Dionysius; he looked on all as rivals, not the adversary alone but the very judge, so that he even repented of having too rashly disclosed these things to Pharnaces, when he might have slept and kept his beloved; for it was not the same thing to guard Callirhoe in Miletus and over all Asia.
7.8. Yet he kept the secret to the end, and did not confess the reason to his wife, but the pretext was that the King was summoning him, wishing to deliberate about the affairs in Ionia. But Callirhoe was grieved, being conveyed far from the Greek sea; for as long as she saw the harbors of Miletus, she thought herself near Syracuse; and she had a great consolation too in the tomb of Chaereas there.

title: Callirhoe
text:
1.1. How Callirhoe was married to Chaereas — the most beautiful of women to the most beautiful of men, the marriage brought about by the contrivance of Aphrodite; and how, when Chaereas in a fit of jealous love had struck her, she seemed to have died, and was buried in great splendour, and then revived in the tomb, where tomb-robbers carried her off from Sicily by night, and sailing to Ionia sold her to Dionysius; and Dionysius's love, and Callirhoe's faithfulness to Chaereas, and the necessity that forced her into marriage for the sake of the child in her womb, and the confession of Theron, and Chaereas's voyage in search of his wife, his capture and his sale into Caria together with his friend Polycharmus —
1.2. and how Mithridates recognized Chaereas when he was about to be put to death, and how he was eager to restore the lovers to each other; and how Dionysius, detecting this from the letters, slandered him to Pharnaces, and Pharnaces to the King, and the King summoned them both to judgment — all this has been set out in the previous book. What followed I shall now relate.
1.3. As far as Syria and Cilicia Callirhoe bore the journey lightly, for she still heard the Greek tongue and could see the sea that led to Syracuse. But when she came to the river Euphrates, beyond which lies the vast mainland that is the starting-point for the King's great empire, then at last a longing for her homeland and her kindred stole over her, with the despair of ever returning.
1.4. Standing on the shore, she ordered everyone to withdraw except Plangon, the one person she trusted, and began to speak in this way: "Spiteful Fortune, who make war upon a single woman with such persistence — you shut me up alive in a tomb, and you brought me out of it not in pity, but to hand me over to pirates.
1.5. The sea and Theron divided my exile between them. I, the daughter of Hermocrates, was sold; and, what was heavier to me than slavery, I was loved, so that, while Chaereas still lived, I should be married to another. Now you even grudge me this, for you no longer banish me only to Ionia. You gave me a foreign land, but a Greek one, where I had this great comfort, that I sat beside the sea. Now you cast me out beyond the air I know, and I am cut off from my homeland by a whole world.
1.6. You have taken Miletus from me, as before you took Syracuse. I am carried off beyond the Euphrates and shut away in the recesses of the barbarians — I, an islander, where there is no longer any sea. What ship can I still hope for, sailing down from Sicily? I am torn even from your tomb, Chaereas.
1.7. Who will bring the offerings to you now, my good spirit? Bactra and Susa are henceforth to be my home and my grave. Once only, Euphrates, am I to cross you; for I dread not so much the length of the journey as the fear that even there I may seem beautiful to someone." So saying, she kissed the ground; then, stepping into the ferry, she crossed over.
1.8. Now Dionysius too had ample provision, for he displayed his riches lavishly to his wife in the equipment of the journey; but the friendliness of the natives made their travel more royal still. People escorted them from town to town, and one satrap handed them on to the next, for her beauty won everyone over. And another hope warmed the barbarians as well — that this woman would have great power — and so each was eager to give gifts of hospitality, or in any case to lay up some claim to her gratitude.
2.1. So matters stood with them. Mithridates, meanwhile, was making his way through Armenia in great haste, chiefly because he feared that this very thing might be made a charge against him before the King — that he had followed close upon the woman's track — but also because he was eager to arrive first and prepare his case for the trial.

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.2. When he reached Babylon, where the King was then staying, he rested that first day in his own quarters, for all the satraps have lodgings assigned to them. On the next day he came to the King's gates, greeted the Persian nobles of equal rank, and honoured first with gifts Artaxates the eunuch, who stood highest and most powerful in the King's favour. Then he said, "Report to the King: Mithridates, your servant, has come to clear himself of a Greek's slander, and to do homage."
2.3. Not long afterward the eunuch came out and answered, "It is the King's will that Mithridates should suffer no wrong; he will give judgment when Dionysius too has arrived." So Mithridates did homage and withdrew. When he was alone, he called Chaereas and said to him, "I am on trial, and the charge against me is that I wished to restore Callirhoe to you. For Dionysius claims that the letter you wrote to your wife was written by me, and he takes it as proof of adultery. He is convinced that you are dead; and let him stay convinced of it until the trial, so that you may appear suddenly.
2.4. This is the return I ask of you for the kindness I have done: hide yourself; bear not to see Callirhoe, nor to ask anything about her." Reluctantly, but obediently, Chaereas agreed and tried to keep out of sight; yet the tears ran down his cheeks. And saying, "I will do, master, what you command," he went off to the chamber where he was lodging with his friend Polycharmus, and flinging himself to the floor, tearing his tunic, "with both his hands he seized the grimy ash and poured it on his head, and fouled his comely face." Then, weeping, he said: "We are near each other, Callirhoe, and we do not see each other.
2.5. You indeed do no wrong, for you do not know that Chaereas is alive; but I am the most impious of all men, since I have been forbidden to look on you, and, coward that I am and clinging to life, I endure this tyranny so far. If anyone had laid such a command on you, you would not have lived."
2.6. So Polycharmus tried to console him. By now Dionysius too was drawing near Babylon, and rumour ran ahead through the city, telling everyone that a woman was coming whose beauty was not human but divine — such as the sun looks on nowhere else upon earth. By nature the barbarians are mad for women, so that every house and every alley was filled with talk of her. The rumour reached even the King himself, so that he asked Artaxates the eunuch whether the woman from Miletus had arrived.
2.7. The fame of his wife had long distressed Dionysius — for he had no security in it — but now, when she was about to enter Babylon, he was inflamed all the more. With a groan he said to himself: "This is no longer Miletus, Dionysius, your own city; even there you had to guard against those who plotted against you.
2.8. Reckless man, with no foresight of what is to come — you are bringing Callirhoe into Babylon, where there are so many men like Mithridates! Menelaus could not keep Helen safe in chaste Sparta, but a barbarian shepherd outdid even a king. There are many Parises among the Persians. Do you not see the dangers, the warning signs? Cities come out to meet us, and satraps pay us court.
2.9. She has already grown haughty, and the King has not yet seen her. One hope of safety remains: to steal the woman away from sight; for she will be guarded if she can stay hidden." With this reasoning he mounted his horse, but left Callirhoe in the covered carriage and closed up the curtain. And perhaps he would have succeeded in what he wished, had not something of this kind happened.

title: Callirhoe
text:
3.1. There came to Statira, the King's wife, the women of the most distinguished Persians, and one of them said: "Mistress, a little Greek woman is making war upon our households — one whom everyone has long admired for her beauty, but now there is danger that in our day the reputation of Persian women may be overthrown. Come, then, let us consider how we may not be outshone by the foreigner."
3.2. The queen laughed, putting no trust in the rumour, and at the same time said: "The Greeks are boastful and poor, and for that reason they marvel greatly at small things. So they cry up Callirhoe as beautiful, just as they cry up Dionysius as rich. Let one of us, then, when she comes in, appear beside her, so as to put the poor slave in the shade."
3.3. All did homage to the queen, marvelled at her judgment, and at first cried out as with one mouth, "If only it were possible for you to be seen, mistress!" Then their opinions divided, and they named the most distinguished women for beauty.
3.4. There was a show of hands as in a theatre, and Rhodogune was chosen — daughter of Zopyrus, wife of Megabyzus — a great and famous creature; what Callirhoe was to Ionia, that Rhodogune was to Asia. The women took her and adorned her, each contributing something of her own to her adornment; and the queen gave her bracelets and a necklace.
3.5. When they had fitly equipped her for the contest, she went out as though to meet Callirhoe — and indeed she had a fitting pretext, since she was the sister of Pharnaces, who had written to the King about Dionysius.
3.6. All Babylon poured out for the spectacle, and the crowd choked the gates. In the most conspicuous place Rhodogune waited, escorted in royal style, standing delicate and languid and as though issuing a challenge; and everyone gazed at her and said to one another, "We have won; the Persian woman will eclipse the foreigner.
3.7. If she can, let her be matched against her; let the Greeks learn that they are boasters." Meanwhile Dionysius came up, and when it was announced to him that the kinswoman of Pharnaces was there, he leapt down from his horse and approached her with courtesy.
3.8. Blushing deeply, she said, "I wish to greet my sister," and at the same moment went up to the carriage. Now it was no longer possible for Callirhoe to stay hidden, and so Dionysius, against his will and groaning with embarrassment, begged Callirhoe to come forward. At once everyone strained not only their eyes but their very souls, and all but fell over one another, each wanting to see before his neighbour and to get as close as he could.
3.9. Callirhoe's face shone out, and its brilliance held all their gazes, as when in deep night a great light suddenly appears. Astonished, the barbarians did homage, and no one seemed to be aware that Rhodogune was there. And Rhodogune herself understood her defeat, and, since she could neither go away nor wished to be looked at, she slipped under the carriage curtain together with Callirhoe,
3.10. surrendering herself to be carried off by her superior. The carriage went on, all curtained over, and the people, no longer able to see Callirhoe, kissed the chariot. When the King heard that Dionysius had arrived, he ordered Artaxates the eunuch to tell him: "You ought not to have delayed in accusing a man entrusted with a great command; but I forgive you the fault, since you were travelling with a woman.
3.11. As for me, I am now keeping a festival and engaged in the sacrifices; on the thirtieth day from now I shall hear the case." Dionysius did homage and departed.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.1. From then on preparation went forward for the trial on both sides, as for the greatest of wars. The mass of the barbarians was divided: the satraps' party sided with Mithridates — for he too was originally from Bactra, though he had later been settled in Caria — while Dionysius had the common people in his favour, since he seemed to be wronged contrary to the laws, having been plotted against in the matter of his wife, and — what is greater — such a wife.
4.2. Nor, indeed, was the women's quarter of the Persians free from concern; here too their zeal was divided. Those who prided themselves on their beauty envied Callirhoe and wished her to be put to shame at the trial, while the majority, envious of their own women, joined in praying that the foreigner might triumph.
4.3. Each of the two men supposed he had victory in his hands. Dionysius was confident in the letters that Mithridates had written to Callirhoe in the name of Chaereas — for he never expected Chaereas to be alive — while Mithridates, having Chaereas to produce, was convinced that he could not be convicted. Yet he pretended to be afraid and called in advocates, so that, by the unexpectedness of it, he might make his defence the more brilliant.
4.4. During those thirty days the Persian men and women talked of nothing else but this trial, so that — if the truth must be told — all Babylon was a courtroom. The interval seemed long to everyone, and not only to the rest but to the King himself. What Olympic games or Eleusinian nights ever roused so great an expectation of eagerness?
4.5. When the appointed day came, the King took his seat. There is in the palace a chamber set apart expressly for a court of justice, surpassing in size and beauty; in the centre stands the throne for the King, and on either side seats for his friends — those who excel in dignity and merit — leaders of leaders.
4.6. Around the throne stand in a circle the captains and commanders and the most honoured of the King's freedmen, so that of that assembly one might fitly say: "And the gods sat in council beside Zeus." Those who take their seats are led in with silence and awe.
4.7. So at dawn Mithridates came first, attended by friends and kinsmen — not at all splendid or cheerful, but, as one on trial, an object of pity. After him came Dionysius too, in Greek dress, clothed in a Milesian robe, holding the letters in his hand.
4.8. When they had been brought in, they did homage. Then the King ordered the secretary to read the letters — that of Pharnaces and the one he himself had written in reply — so that those who sat in judgment with him might learn how the matter had been brought forward. When the letters had been read, a great burst of praise broke out from those who marvelled at the King's wisdom and justice.
4.9. When silence had fallen, Dionysius the accuser ought to have begun his speech, and everyone looked toward him. But Mithridates said: "I do not forestall my defence, master, but I know the proper order; before the speeches all who are essential to the case must be present. Where, then, is the woman about whom the trial is held? You judged her essential by the letter, and wrote that she should be present, and she is present.
4.10. Let not Dionysius, then, conceal the chief point and the cause of the whole matter." To this Dionysius answered: "This too is the act of an adulterer — to drag another man's wife before the crowd against her husband's will, when she is neither accusing nor being accused.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.11. If she had been seduced, she would have had to be present as one liable; but as it is, you plotted against her without her knowledge, and I use the woman neither as witness nor as advocate. Why then must she be present who has no share at all in the trial?" This Dionysius said in lawyer's fashion, yet he persuaded no one;
4.12. for everyone longed to see Callirhoe. Since the King was ashamed to give the order, his friends made the letter their pretext, for she had been summoned as essential. "How, then, is it not absurd," said one, "that she should come from Ionia, and yet, being in Babylon, be absent?" So when it was decreed that Callirhoe too should be present, Dionysius, having told her nothing beforehand but having concealed to the very last the reason for the journey to Babylon, and fearing to bring her suddenly into court knowing nothing — for the woman was likely to be indignant at having been deceived — postponed the trial to the next day.
5.1. And so for that day they were dismissed. When Dionysius came home, like the prudent and educated man he was, he laid before his wife the most persuasive account possible in such circumstances, relating each thing gently and mildly. Yet not without tears did Callirhoe hear it; at the name of Chaereas she wept much, and at the trial she was distressed.
5.2. "This alone," she said, "was wanting to my misfortunes — to come into a court of law. I have died and been buried, my tomb has been robbed, I have been sold, I have been a slave; and now, see, Fortune, I am put on trial as well. It was not enough for you to slander me unjustly to Chaereas — you have given me to Dionysius as a pretext for a charge of adultery.
5.3. Once you paraded your slander of me at a tomb, now before a royal court. I have become a tale told in Asia and in Europe. With what eyes shall I look upon the judge? What words must I hear? Beauty that lies in wait, given me by nature for this alone — that I should be filled with slanders.
5.4. The daughter of Hermocrates is on trial, and has not her father for advocate. When others go into a court, they pray for goodwill and favour; but I am afraid that I may please the judge."
5.5. Lamenting in this way, she passed the whole day in dejection, and Dionysius more than she. When night came on, she dreamed she saw herself in Syracuse as a maiden, entering the precinct of Aphrodite and returning from it, seeing Chaereas, and the whole city garlanded on her wedding day, and herself escorted by her father and mother to the bridegroom's house.
5.6. As she was about to kiss Chaereas, she started up out of sleep, and calling Plangon — for Dionysius had already risen early to rehearse his case — she told the dream. And Plangon answered: "Take heart, mistress, and rejoice; you have seen a good dream. You will be freed from all your cares;
5.7. for as it seemed to you in the dream, so it shall be in waking life. Go to the King's court as to a temple of Aphrodite; remember yourself; take up again your bridal beauty." And so saying, she dressed and adorned Callirhoe, who of her own accord had a cheerful spirit, as though foreseeing what was to come.
5.8. At dawn, then, there was a crush about the palace, and the alleys were full right out to their ends; for everyone came running, in seeming to be hearers of the trial, but in truth to be spectators of Callirhoe. And by as much as she had before surpassed other women, by so much she now seemed to surpass herself.
5.9. So she entered the court, such as the divine poet says Helen appeared to those about Priam, "Panthoos and Thymoetes, elders of the people"; and at the sight of her there was wonder and silence, and "all prayed to lie beside her in her bed." Indeed, had Mithridates been required to speak first, he could have found no voice; for, as upon an old wound, his amorous desire received once more a sharper blow.

title: Callirhoe
text:
6.1. Dionysius began his speech thus: "I am grateful to you, King, for the honour you have shown me, and to chastity, and to the marriages of all men; for you did not overlook a private man plotted against by a governor, but summoned us, so that in my case you might punish the wantonness and outrage,
6.2. and deter all others from it. And the deed has become worthy of a greater punishment because of the man who did it. For Mithridates, being no enemy but my guest-friend, plotted against me, and not against any other of my possessions, but against what is dearer to me than body and soul — my wife.
6.3. He, of all men, ought, if anyone else had wronged us, to have come to my aid himself, if not for my sake as a friend, then for yours as King. For you placed in his hands the greatest command, and, showing himself unworthy of it, he disgraced it — or rather, betrayed the one who entrusted him with that command.
