6.4. As for the entreaties of Mithridates, and the power, and all the preparation he has brought to bear upon this contest, since we do not stand on equal terms, I myself am not unaware of it; but I am confident, King, in your justice, and in marriage, and in the laws, which you keep alike for all.
6.5. For if you mean to acquit him, it would have been far better not to have summoned him at all; for at that time everyone was afraid, supposing that his wantonness would be punished if it came to trial — whereas hereafter he will hold the law in contempt, if, judged before you, he goes unpunished. My own argument is clear and brief. I am the husband of this woman, Callirhoe, and by now a father by her; I married her not as a maiden but after she had belonged to a former husband, Chaereas by name, long since dead,
6.6. whose tomb also stands among us. Now Mithridates, when he came to Miletus and saw my wife in accordance with the rights of hospitality, did not behave thereafter either as a friend or as a self-controlled and decent man — such as you wish those to be to whom your cities are entrusted — but showed himself wanton and tyrannical.
6.7. Knowing the chastity and love of husband in the woman, he judged it impossible to persuade her by words or money, and so devised a stratagem of treachery which he thought most persuasive: he pretended that her former husband Chaereas was alive, and, forging letters in his name to Callirhoe, sent them by slaves.
6.8. But your fortune, King, since he was a worthy man, set him on his way, and the providence of the other gods made the plot plain; for the slaves with the letters were sent to me by Bias, the general of the Prienians, and I, having detected them, informed the satrap of Lydia and Ionia, Pharnaces, and he informed you.
6.9. I have now told the story of the matter on which you are giving judgment; and the proofs are inescapable. For one of two things must be true: either Chaereas is alive, or Mithridates is convicted of adultery. And he cannot even say that he was ignorant of Chaereas's death; for while Chaereas was present in Miletus we heaped up the tomb for him, and he mourned along with us.
6.10. But whenever Mithridates wishes to commit adultery, he raises the dead. I shall finish when I have read the letter which he sent through his own slaves to Miletus from Caria. Take it and read: 'Chaereas, I am alive.' Let Mithridates prove this and be acquitted. Consider, King, how shameless an adulterer is, when he lies even about a dead man."
6.11. With these words Dionysius stirred up his hearers and at once had the vote in his favour; and the King, growing angry, looked bitterly and grimly upon Mithridates.

title: Callirhoe
text:
7.1. But Mithridates, not at all dismayed, said: "I beg you, King — for you are just and humane — do not condemn me before you hear the arguments on both sides, and do not let a Greek, who has craftily put together false slanders against me, prove more persuasive with you than the truth.
7.2. I understand that the woman's beauty weighs against me toward suspicion; for it seems incredible to no one that someone should wish to seduce Callirhoe. But I have lived the rest of my life chastely, and this is the first charge I have faced; and even had I been licentious and wanton, the very fact that so many cities have been entrusted to me by you would have made me a better man.
7.3. Who is so foolish as to choose to lose such great blessings for the sake of one pleasure — and a shameful one at that? And indeed, if I were conscious of any wrongdoing in myself, I could even have challenged the jurisdiction of this trial; for Dionysius does not bring his charge on behalf of a wife married to him according to law, but he bought her when she was being sold — and the law of adultery does not apply to slaves.
7.4. Let him first read you the deed of manumission, and then let him speak of marriage. Do you dare to call her a wife, whom Theron the pirate sold to you for a talent, and he himself having snatched her from a tomb? 'But,' you say, 'I bought her as a free woman.' Then you are a kidnapper, and not a husband. Yet I shall now make my defence to you as to a husband.
7.5. Reckon the sale a marriage, and the price a dowry; let the woman of Syracuse pass today for a Milesian. Learn, master, that I have wronged Dionysius neither as a husband nor as a master. First, he charges me with an adultery not committed but only intended, and, having no act to allege, he reads out empty documents.
7.6. The laws inflict their penalties for deeds. You produce a letter. I could say: 'I did not write it; you have no writing of mine; it is Chaereas who seeks Callirhoe — try him, then, for adultery.' 'Yes,' you say, 'but Chaereas is dead, and you, in the name of the dead man, corrupted my wife.' You challenge me, Dionysius,
7.7. with a challenge in no way to your advantage. I call it to witness: I am your friend and guest. Withdraw from the accusation; it is to your advantage. Beg the King to dismiss the case. Sing your recantation: 'Mithridates does no wrong; in vain did I blame him.' But if you persist, you will repent; you will be casting the vote against yourself. I warn you, you will lose Callirhoe. It is not I whom the King will find an adulterer, but another."
7.8. Having said this, he fell silent; and everyone looked toward Dionysius, wishing to learn, now that the choice had been set before him, whether he would withdraw from the accusation or hold firmly to it. For what Mithridates was hinting at they themselves did not understand, but supposed that Dionysius knew. And he too was ignorant of it, never having hoped that Chaereas was alive.
7.9. So he said: "Say whatever you wish; you will not deceive me with sophistries and plausible threats, nor will Dionysius ever be found to be a false accuser."
7.10. Taking his cue from this, Mithridates raised his voice and, as if for a solemn invocation, said: "Gods of the royal house, both heavenly and beneath the earth, come to the aid of a good man, who has often prayed to you righteously and sacrificed magnificently. Grant me the reward of my piety, now that I am falsely accused. Lend me, if only for this trial, Chaereas. Appear, good spirit; your own Callirhoe calls you. And standing between us both, me and Dionysius, tell the King which of us is the adulterer."

title: Callirhoe
text:
8.1. While he was still speaking — for so it had been arranged — Chaereas himself came forward. And when Callirhoe saw him she cried out, "Chaereas, are you alive?" and rushed to run to him; but Dionysius held her back, and placing himself between them, did not let them embrace each other.
8.2. Who could fittingly describe that scene in the court? What poet ever brought so strange a story upon the stage? You would have thought you were present in a theatre filled with a thousand passions: all were there at once — tears, joy, wonder, pity,
8.3. disbelief, prayers. They called Chaereas blessed, rejoiced with Mithridates, grieved with Dionysius, and were at a loss about Callirhoe. For she above all was in confusion, and stood speechless, only gazing at Chaereas with wide-open eyes. I think even the King himself would have wished then to be Chaereas.
8.4. Now war between rivals is familiar and ready to hand for all; but in their case the prize being visible inflamed their rivalry against each other all the more, so that, had it not been for their respect for the King, they would have come to blows.
8.5. As it was, they went as far as words. Chaereas said, "I am the first husband." Dionysius said, "I am the more secure." "Did I ever let my wife go?" "But you buried her." "Show the dissolution of the marriage." "You see the tomb." "Her father gave her to me." "She gave herself to me." "You are unworthy of the daughter of Hermocrates." "You more so — you who were bound in chains by Mithridates." "I demand Callirhoe back." "And I keep her." "You hold another man's wife." "You killed your own."
8.6. "Adulterer." "Murderer." Thus they fought with one another, and all the rest listened not without pleasure. Callirhoe stood looking down and weeping, loving Chaereas, ashamed before Dionysius. The King removed everyone and took counsel with his friends — no longer about Mithridates, for he had brilliantly cleared himself, but whether he should set up a separate trial concerning the woman.
8.7. Some thought the case was not one for a king: "You rightly heard the accusation against Mithridates, for he was a satrap; but these men are all private persons." The majority, however, advised the opposite, both because of the woman's father, who had been of no little use to the royal house, and because the King would not be calling the case before himself from outside, but it was practically a part of the one he was already judging. The truest reason they were unwilling to confess — that Callirhoe's beauty was hard for those who saw it to tear themselves from.
8.8. So, calling back those he had dismissed, he said: "I acquit Mithridates, and let him depart tomorrow to his own satrapy, having received gifts from me. Let Chaereas and Dionysius each state what claims he has concerning the woman; for I must take thought for the daughter of Hermocrates, who utterly defeated the Athenians,
8.9. the bitterest enemies both to me and to the Persians." When this decision had been spoken, Mithridates did homage, but perplexity seized the others. Seeing them at a loss, the King said: "I am not pressing you, but I grant you leave to come to the trial after you have prepared yourselves. I give you an interval of five days; and in the meantime my wife Statira shall take care of Callirhoe. For it is not right that, when she is about to be judged concerning a husband, she should come to the trial with a husband."
8.10. So they went out of the court, all the others downcast, and Mithridates alone rejoicing. Having received his gifts and stayed the night, at dawn he set out for Caria more splendid than before.

title: Callirhoe
text:
9.1. As for Callirhoe, eunuchs took her and led her to the queen, telling her nothing beforehand; for when the King sends someone, no announcement is made. Seeing her suddenly, Statira sprang up from her couch, thinking that Aphrodite stood before her — for she honoured the goddess especially.
9.2. And Callirhoe did homage. The eunuch, perceiving her astonishment, said: "This is Callirhoe; the King has sent her, so that she may be kept with you until the trial." Statira was glad to hear this, and, laying aside all womanly rivalry, became more kindly disposed to Callirhoe because of the honour done her;
9.3. for she took pride in the charge entrusted to her. Taking her by the hand, she said: "Take heart, woman, and cease your weeping. The King is kind. You shall have the husband you wish; you will be married more honourably after the trial. Go now and rest, for you are weary, as I see, and your soul is still troubled." Callirhoe was glad to hear this, for she longed for quiet.
9.4. So when she had lain down and they let her rest, touching her eyes she said: "Did you truly see Chaereas? Was that my Chaereas, or am I deceived in this too? For perhaps Mithridates, for the sake of the trial, sent a phantom; they say there are magi among the Persians.
9.5. And yet he spoke, and said everything as one who knew. How then did he bear not to embrace me? We parted without even kissing each other." While she was reasoning thus, there was heard a sound of feet and the cries of women; for all came running to the queen, thinking they had ample licence to see Callirhoe.
9.6. But Statira said: "Let us leave her, for she is in a poor state; we have days enough both to see and to hear and to talk." Sorrowing, they went away, and at dawn the next day they came again; and this was done on all the days with eagerness, so that the King's house became more crowded than ever.
9.7. Indeed, even the King came in to the women more often, ostensibly to visit Statira. Costly gifts were sent to Callirhoe, but she accepted them from no one, keeping the bearing of an unfortunate woman — dressed in black, unadorned, sitting still. This made her shine all the more brightly. When the queen asked which of the two husbands she preferred, she answered nothing, but only wept.
9.8. Such was Callirhoe's state. Dionysius, for his part, tried to bear what was happening nobly, both through the steadiness of his nature and through the care of his education; but the strangeness of the calamity was powerful enough to unsettle even a brave man.
9.9. For he burned more fiercely than at Miletus. When his desire began, he was a lover of her beauty alone; but now many things kindled his love still further — familiarity, the blessing of children, ingratitude, jealousy, and most of all the unexpectedness of it.
10.1. So suddenly he would often cry out: "What Protesilaus is this who has come to life again to thwart me? What god beneath the earth have I offended, that I should find a dead man for my rival in love — a man whose tomb I keep? Lady Aphrodite, you have ensnared me — you whom I set up among my own household gods, to whom I sacrifice so often. Why did you show me Callirhoe, whom you did not mean to keep for me?
10.2. Why did you make me a father, when I am not even a husband?" Meanwhile, embracing his son, he said weeping: "Wretched child, who once seemed to me born in good fortune, but now in an evil hour; for in you I have an inheritance from your mother and a memorial of an unhappy love.

title: Callirhoe
text:
10.3. You are but a little child, yet not wholly insensible of your father's misfortunes. We came on an ill journey; I should not have left Miletus. Babylon has been our ruin. In the first trial I have been beaten; Mithridates accused me. As for the second, I am more afraid; for the danger is no less, and the outcome of the first has made me despair of the trial.
10.4. Without a trial I have been deprived of my wife, and now I contend for my own wife against another; and — what is harder than this — I do not know whom Callirhoe wishes. But you, my child, can learn from your mother. Go now and plead on your father's behalf.
10.5. Weep, kiss her, say: 'Mother, my father loves you,' and reproach her with nothing. What do you say, attendant? No one allows you to enter the palace? O dreadful tyranny — they shut out a son who comes as an ambassador from his father to his mother."
10.6. So Dionysius passed the time until the trial, arbitrating a battle between love and reason; but Chaereas was held by inconsolable grief. Pretending to be ill, he ordered Polycharmus to escort Mithridates, as the benefactor of them both; and when he was alone, he fastened a noose, and as he was about to climb up to it, he said: "I should have died more happily had I climbed the cross which a false accusation set up for me when I was bound in Caria; for then I would have departed from life still deceived into thinking I was loved by Callirhoe, whereas now I have lost not only life but the consolation of death as well.
10.7. Callirhoe, when she saw me, did not come to me, did not kiss me; with me standing by, she felt shame before another. Let her feel no awkwardness on my account: I will forestall the trial; I will not wait for an inglorious end. I know that I am a weak antagonist for Dionysius — a foreigner and a poor man and now another's. May you be fortunate, woman; for I call you wife, even though you love another. I am departing, and I do not trouble your marriage. Be rich and live in luxury and enjoy the wealth of Ionia. Keep whom you wish.
10.8. But now, when Chaereas is truly dead, I ask of you, Callirhoe, a last favour. When I am dead, come to my body, and if you can, weep — for that will be to me greater than immortality; and bending over my gravestone, even though your husband and your child look on, say: 'You are gone, Chaereas, now truly; now you have died; for I was about to choose you before the King.'
10.9. I shall hear you, woman; perhaps I shall even believe you. You will make me more honoured among the spirits below: 'Even if the dead forget in the house of Hades, yet even there will I remember my dear companion.'" Lamenting in this way, he kissed the noose, saying: "You are my comfort and my advocate; through you I conquer;
10.10. you have loved me more than Callirhoe has." As he was climbing up and fastening it about his neck, his friend Polycharmus came upon him and held him back as one out of his mind, no longer able to console him. And by now the appointed day for the trial had arrived.
1.1. When the King was to give judgment the next day whether Callirhoe ought to be the wife of Chaereas or of Dionysius, all Babylon was in suspense; both in their houses, as they spoke to one another, and in the streets, those who met would say: "Tomorrow are Callirhoe's nuptials.
1.2. Who, then, is the more fortunate?" The city was divided. Those who took Chaereas's part would say: "He was the first husband; he married her a maiden, a lover loving one who loved him; her father gave her to him, his country buried her; he did not abandon the marriage, he was deprived of it. But Dionysius bought her, he did not marry her; pirates sold her; and it is not lawful to buy a free woman."

title: Callirhoe
text:
1.3. Those who took Dionysius's part argued back in turn: "He rescued her from pirates when she was on the very point of being murdered; he gave a talent for her safety; first he saved her, then he married her; but Chaereas, having married her, killed her. Callirhoe ought to remember the marriage. And Dionysius has this further advantage toward winning,
1.4. that they also have a child in common." So spoke the men. The women not only made speeches, but also gave advice as if she were present: "Callirhoe, do not abandon your first love; choose the one who first kissed you, your fellow-citizen, so that you may see your father again; otherwise you will live in a foreign land as an exile."
1.5. But others said: "Choose your benefactor, the one who saved you, not the one who killed you. What if Chaereas should grow angry again? Again a tomb. Do not betray your son; honour the father of your child." Such things one might hear them saying, so that anyone would have said all Babylon was a courtroom.
1.6. That last night before the trial had come. The royal pair lay down with thoughts that were not alike: the queen prayed for day to come more quickly, that she might lay aside the charge entrusted to her as a burden — for the beauty of the woman, set in close comparison, weighed upon her; and she had begun to suspect the King's frequent visits and his ill-timed attentions.
1.7. For before this he rarely went into the women's quarter; but ever since he had Callirhoe within, he came continually. She watched him too in their conversations, quietly stealing glances at Callirhoe, and his eyes pretending to look away but of their own accord drawn there.
1.8. So Statira awaited a pleasant day, but the King not such a one. All night long he lay awake, now on his side, now on his face, pondering within himself and saying: "The trial is at hand; for in my rashness I set a short interval. What, then, are we to do at dawn? Callirhoe will go off henceforth, either to Miletus or to Syracuse.
1.9. Unhappy eyes, you have one hour left to enjoy the fairest of sights; then a slave of mine will become more fortunate than I. Consider what you must do, my soul; come to yourself; you have no other counsellor. Love himself is love's counsellor.
1.10. First, then, answer your own self: who are you? Callirhoe's lover or her judge? Do not deceive yourself. You deny it, but you are in love; you will be convicted all the more when you no longer see her. What then? Do you wish to grieve yourself? The Sun, your forefather, has singled out for you this living being, the fairest of those on which he himself looks down; and will you drive away the god's gift?
1.11. As if I greatly cared about Chaereas and Dionysius, my own obscure slaves, that I should arbitrate their marriage, and that I, the Great King, should perform the work of an old matchmaking woman! But I have already undertaken the case, and everyone knows it.
1.12. Most of all I feel shame before Statira. So do not make your love public, nor bring the trial to its conclusion. It is enough for you even to look at Callirhoe; postpone the judgment — for this much is permitted even to a private judge."
2.1. So when day appeared, the attendants made ready the royal court; and the multitude came running to the palace, and all Babylon was in a stir. Just as at the Olympic games one may watch the athletes coming to the stadium with an escort, so it was with these men too. The most distinguished body of the Persians escorted Dionysius, and the common people Chaereas.

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.2. There were countless joint prayers and shouts from those who took the side of each, acclaiming them: "You are the better; you will win." But the prize was no wild-olive wreath, no apples, no pine garland, but beauty in the first rank, over which even the gods might justly have contended. The King called the eunuch Artaxates, who stood highest with him, and said: "The gods of the royal house appeared to me in a dream demanding sacrifice, and I must first fulfil the duties of piety.
2.3. Proclaim, then, a sacred month of thirty days' festival for all Asia, free of lawsuits and business." The eunuch announced the order, and at once everything was full of people sacrificing, garlanded.
2.4. The pipe sounded, the syrinx shrilled, the song's melody was heard; incense smoked at the doorways, and every alley was a banquet; "and the savour of the offering rose to heaven, wreathed about with smoke." The King set magnificent sacrifices upon the altars. Then for the first time he sacrificed also to Love, and earnestly entreated Aphrodite to help him with her son.
2.5. While all were in good cheer, three alone were grieving: Callirhoe, Dionysius, and before them both Chaereas. Callirhoe could not grieve openly in the palace, but quietly and unseen she sighed and cursed the festival. Dionysius grieved at himself, because he had left Miletus. "Bear," he said, "wretched man, your self-chosen misfortune; for you yourself are the cause of these things.
2.6. You might have kept Callirhoe even while Chaereas was alive. You were master in Miletus, and not even the letter would then have been given to Callirhoe against your will. Who would have seen it? Who would have approached her? But you took yourself and flung yourself into the midst of your enemies.
2.7. And would that you had thrown yourself alone; but now you have flung in too the possession dearer to you than your own soul. For this reason war has been stirred up against you from every side. Why do you go to law, fool? You have Chaereas as your opponent; you have made for yourself a master to be your rival in love. Now the King even sees dreams, and the very gods to whom he sacrifices daily demand sacrifices of him.
2.8. Oh, the shamelessness! Someone drags out the trial while keeping another man's wife within, and such a man claims to be a judge." So Dionysius lamented. But Chaereas would not touch food, and had no wish at all to live. When his friend Polycharmus tried to keep him from starving himself, "You," he said, "are to me of all men the most hostile under the guise of a friend; for you hold me back while I am being tortured, and you look on with pleasure while I am punished.
2.9. If you were a friend, you would not begrudge me freedom when I am tyrannized over by an evil spirit. How many chances of good fortune have you destroyed for me? I would have been happy, had I been buried together with Callirhoe when she was buried in Syracuse; but even then you held me back, though I wished to die, and robbed me of a fair companionship; for perhaps she would not have left the tomb, abandoning the dead man.
2.10. But suppose I had lain there — afterward I would have gained this much: the sale, the pirates' den, the chains, and a King harder than the cross. O fair death, after which I heard of Callirhoe's second marriage! What an opportunity for starving myself you destroyed again — the one after the trial!
2.11. I saw Callirhoe and did not go to her, did not kiss her. Oh, a strange and incredible thing — Chaereas is on trial as to whether he is Callirhoe's husband! But the spiteful spirit will not allow even the trial, such as it is, to be brought to completion. Both in dreams and waking the gods hate me." Saying this, he rushed for his sword, but Polycharmus held back his hand, and all but binding him, kept guard over him.

title: Callirhoe
text:
3.1. The King called the eunuch, who was the most trusted of all to him, but at first felt shame even before him. Seeing him full of blushes and wishing to speak, Artaxates said: "Why do you hide it, master, from your slave, who is loyal to you and able to keep silence? What so dreadful thing has happened? How anxious I am, lest some plot..." The King said: "Yes, and the greatest plot, but not by men — by a god.
3.2. Who Love is, I had heard before in tales and poems — that he rules over all the gods and over Zeus himself; yet I did not believe that anyone could become, in my presence, more powerful than I. But the god is here; he has taken up his dwelling in my soul, mighty and overwhelming. I love — it is shameful to confess, but truly I have been taken captive."
3.3. As he said this he filled with tears, so that he could add nothing more to his words. When he fell silent, Artaxates at once understood from where he had been wounded; for he had not been without suspicion before, but had perceived the fire smouldering; and indeed it was neither doubtful nor unclear that, with Callirhoe present, he would have loved no other.
3.4. Yet he pretended ignorance and said: "What beauty can master your soul, my lord, to which all fair things are slaves? Gold, silver, raiment, horses, cities, nations; countless beautiful women, but Statira above all, the fairest under the sun, whom you alone enjoy. Power dissolves love — unless some other Thetis has come down from heaven above or risen from the sea.
3.5. For I believe that even gods desire your company." The King answered: "Perhaps what you say is true, that this woman is one of the gods; for her beauty is not human. Yet she does not admit it. She pretends to be a Greek of Syracuse. And this too is a sign of her deceit.
3.6. For she does not wish to be exposed by naming a city among those subject to us, but sends the tale of herself out beyond the Ionian Sea and the wide ocean. On the pretext of a lawsuit she came to me, and she contrived this whole drama. I wonder at you, how you dared to call Statira fairest of all, while you look at Callirhoe.
3.7. We must consider, then, how I might be rid of this distress. Search everywhere, in case some remedy can be found." "A remedy has been found, King," he said, "the very one you seek, both among Greeks and barbarians. For there is no other remedy for Love than the beloved himself; this too is the oracle that is sung, that the one who wounds shall himself heal." The King felt shame at the words and said: "Do not say any such thing — that I should corrupt another man's wife.
3.8. I remember the laws I myself laid down, and the justice I practise in all things. Do not condemn me for any incontinence. I am not so far taken." Afraid that he had spoken something rash, Artaxates turned his speech into praise. "You think nobly, King," he said. "Do not bring to Love the same treatment as other men do, but the higher, the royal kind — contending against your own self; for you alone, master,
3.9. are able to master even a god. Lead your soul away into every pleasure. Above all you delight especially in hunting. For I know that, for the pleasure of it, you pass whole days without eating or drinking. To linger in the hunt is better than to be in the palace and near the fire."
4.1. This was pleasing, and a magnificent hunt was proclaimed. Out rode horsemen in their finery, the best of the Persians and the chosen flower of the rest of the army. And though all were a sight worth seeing, the most resplendent among them was the King.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.2. For he sat upon a Nisaean horse, the most beautiful and the largest, with a golden bridle, golden cheek-pieces, frontlet and breastplate; he was clothed in Tyrian purple — the weaving was Babylonian — and a tiara dyed with hyacinth. Girt with a golden scimitar, he held two javelins, and a quiver and bow hung at his side, the most costly work of the Chinese.
4.3. He sat there in his pride; for love of finery is proper to love. He wished to be seen by Callirhoe in their midst, and as he rode out through the whole city he looked around to see whether she too was anywhere watching the procession. Quickly the mountains were filled with men shouting, running, dogs barking, horses neighing, beasts being driven.
4.4. That eagerness and tumult would have unsettled even Love himself; for there was delight mixed with struggle, joy mixed with fear, and danger that was sweet. But the King saw no horse, though so many galloped beside him, no wild beast, though so many were being chased, heard no dog, though so many were baying, nor men, though all were shouting.
4.5. He saw only Callirhoe, who was not present, and heard her, who was not speaking. For Love had gone out to the hunt with him, and — being a contentious god — seeing himself opposed and well guarded against, as the King supposed, turned the stratagem against him to the opposite effect, and through the very treatment inflamed his soul, being present within and saying: "What it would be to see Callirhoe here, her legs girded up and her arms bared, her face flushed,
4.6. her breast full of panting. Truly: 'As Artemis goes down the mountain, the showerer of arrows, over towering Taygetus or Erymanthus, delighting in boars and swift deer.'" Painting and shaping these images, he burned more fiercely.
4.7. As he was saying these things, Artaxates broke in: "You have forgotten, master, what has happened. For Callirhoe has no husband, but awaits the judgment of whom she is to marry. Remember, then, that you love a widow; and feel shame neither before the laws — for they are laid down for marriages — nor before adultery, since the man wronged must first be a husband,
4.8. and then the wrongdoer an adulterer." The argument pleased the King, for it was to his pleasure, and taking the eunuch by the hand he kissed him and said: "Justly, then, do I prefer you above all; for you are most loyal to me and a good guardian. Go and bring Callirhoe. Two things I lay upon you: not against her will, and not openly; for I wish you both to persuade her and to escape notice."
4.9. At once, then, the signal to recall the hunt was passed along, and all turned back; and the King, buoyed up by hope, rode into the palace rejoicing as though he had hunted down the fairest quarry.
4.10. And Artaxates too rejoiced, thinking that he had undertaken a service, and that he would henceforth steer a royal chariot, with both grateful to him — but Callirhoe more. He supposed the task an easy one, being a eunuch, a slave, a barbarian. He did not know the noble Greek spirit, and least of all that of Callirhoe, the chaste and husband-loving.
5.1. So, watching for an opportunity, he came to her, and, finding her alone, said: "I have brought you, woman, a treasure of great blessings; only remember my kindness, for I believe you are grateful." At the beginning of his speech Callirhoe became overjoyed; for by nature a person believes that what he wishes is also so.
5.2. She thought, perhaps, that she was to be given back to Chaereas, and was eager to hear this, promising to repay the eunuch for his good news. But he, taking up his preamble again, began: "You, woman, have had the good fortune of a divine beauty, but you have reaped from it nothing great or honourable.

title: Callirhoe
text:
5.3. Your name, glorious and renowned through all the earth, has found to this day neither a husband worthy of it nor a lover, but has fallen to two men, a poor islander, and the other, the King's slave.
5.4. What great and splendid thing has come to you from these? What fruitful land do you possess? What costly adornment? What cities do you rule? How many slaves do homage to you? Babylonian women have maidservants richer than you. Yet you have not been neglected in everything; rather the gods care for you.
5.5. For this reason they brought you here, finding the lawsuit as a pretext, that the Great King might behold you. And this is the first good news you have: he has looked on you with pleasure. And I remind him of you, and praise you in his presence." He added this; for every slave is accustomed, when he speaks to anyone about his master, to recommend himself as well, seeking his own profit from the conversation.
5.6. But Callirhoe's heart was at once struck as though by a sword at his words. She pretended, however, not to understand, and said: "May the gods remain gracious to the King, and he to you, that you pity an unfortunate woman. I beg you, let him quickly free me from my anxiety by bringing the trial to its conclusion, so that I may no longer trouble even the queen." The eunuch, thinking that he had spoken his meaning unclearly and that the woman had not understood, began to speak more plainly.
5.7. "This very thing is your good fortune, that you no longer have slaves and poor men as lovers, but the Great King, who is able to give you Miletus itself and all Ionia and Sicily and other nations greater still. Sacrifice, then, to the gods and count yourself blessed, and see that you please him the more,
5.8. and when you are rich, remember me." Callirhoe at first felt the impulse, if it were possible, even to tear out the eyes of the man who was corrupting her; but, like an educated and sensible woman, quickly reckoning both the place and who she was and who the speaker was, she changed her anger and thereafter played the ironist with the barbarian.
5.9. "May I not be so mad," she said, "as to be persuaded that I am worthy of the Great King. I am like the maidservants of the Persian women. Do not, I beg you, mention me again to your master. For even if at the moment he be not angry, afterward he will be harsh with you, reckoning that you cast the lord of all the earth beneath a slave-woman of Dionysius.
5.10. I wonder that, being most intelligent, you are ignorant of the King's humanity — that he does not love an unfortunate woman, but pities her. Let us cease talking, then, lest someone slander us to the queen." And she ran off, while the eunuch stood agape; for, reared in a great despotism, he supposed nothing impossible, not for the King only, but not even for himself.
6.1. Left behind and not even granted an answer, he went off full of a thousand feelings: angry at Callirhoe, grieved at himself, afraid of the King. For perhaps he would not even believe that he had spoken, however unsuccessfully; and he would seem to be betraying his service to gratify the queen.
6.2. He was afraid, too, lest Callirhoe should report his words to her, and lest Statira, growing indignant, should devise some great evil for him, as one who was not only serving the love but contriving it. So the eunuch considered how he might safely report to the King what had happened; while Callirhoe, being by herself, said: "I foretold this.
6.3. I have you as witness, Euphrates. I declared that I would never cross you again. Farewell, father, and you, mother, and Syracuse my homeland; for I shall see you no more. Now in truth Callirhoe is dead. From the tomb I came out, but henceforth not even Theron the pirate will bring me out of this.

title: Callirhoe
text:
6.4. O treacherous beauty, you are the cause of all my evils. Because of you I was killed, because of you I was sold, because of you I married after Chaereas, because of you I was brought to Babylon, because of you I stood before a tribunal. To how many you have handed me over — to pirates, to the sea, to the tomb, to slavery, to trial! But heaviest of all to me is the King's love.
6.5. And I do not yet speak of the King's anger; more fearful, I think, is the queen's jealousy, which Chaereas, a Greek and a man, could not bear. What will a woman do, and a barbarian mistress? Come then, Callirhoe, resolve on something noble, worthy of Hermocrates: cut your own throat. But not yet; for so far this is only a first conversation, and from a eunuch. If something more violent should happen, then is the time to show Chaereas, when he is present, your faithfulness."
6.6. The eunuch, coming to the King, concealed the truth of what had happened, and pleaded as his excuse the queen's constant occupations and her close watch, so that he could not even approach Callirhoe. "And you ordered me, master, to take care to escape notice.
6.7. And you ordered rightly; for you have taken up the most august character of a judge, and you wish to be well thought of among the Persians. For this reason all sing your praises. But the Greeks are fault-finders and chatterers. They themselves will make the matter notorious — Callirhoe out of vanity, because the King loves her, and Dionysius and Chaereas out of jealousy.
6.8. Nor is it worth grieving even the queen, whom the trial has made seem more beautiful." With these things he mixed in his recantation, in case he could somehow turn the King away from his love and free himself from a troublesome service.
7.1. For the moment, then, he persuaded him; but when night came on again the King kindled once more, and love reminded him what eyes Callirhoe had, how beautiful her face. He praised her hair, her walk, her voice; how she had entered the court, how she had stood, how she had spoken, how she had been silent, how she had rejoiced, how she had wept.
7.2. Lying awake the greater part of the night, and sleeping only so long as even in his dreams to see Callirhoe, at dawn he called the eunuch and said: "Go and watch all day long; for you will surely find some opportunity, however brief, for an unobserved conversation. If I had wished to overcome my desire openly and by force,
7.3. I have my guards." The eunuch did homage and promised; for it is permitted to no one to gainsay the King when he commands. But knowing that Callirhoe would give no opportunity, but would deliberately ward off the conversation by staying with the queen, and wishing to remedy this, he turned the blame not on the one guarded but on the one guarding.
7.4. "If it seem good to you, master," he said, "send for Statira, as though wishing to discuss something privately with her; for her absence will give me access to Callirhoe." "Do so," said the King.
7.5. So Artaxates came and, doing homage to the queen, said: "Your husband calls you, mistress." On hearing this Statira did homage and went off in haste to him. The eunuch, seeing Callirhoe left alone, took her right hand and, as though he were some lover of Greeks and friend to all, led her away from the throng of maidservants.
7.6. She understood, and at once grew pale and speechless, yet followed nonetheless. When they were alone, he said to her: "You saw how the queen, on hearing the King's name, did homage and went off running; but you, a slave, cannot bear good fortune, nor are you content that he should entreat you when he could command.

title: Callirhoe
text:
7.7. But I — for I honour you — did not report your madness to him; on the contrary, I made promises on your behalf. Two roads, then, lie before you. Which do you wish to take? I will tell you both. If you obey the King, you will receive the fairest gifts and a husband of your choice; for he surely does not mean to marry you himself, but you will grant him a passing favour. But if not, you will suffer against your will what the King's enemies suffer; for they alone are not even permitted to die when they wish."
7.8. Callirhoe laughed at the threat and said: "This is not the first time I shall suffer something dreadful; I am experienced in misfortune. What can the King do to me harsher than what I have suffered? I was buried alive; the tomb is narrower than any prison.
7.9. I was handed over to the hands of pirates. Now I suffer the greatest of evils: Chaereas is present, and I do not see him." This word betrayed her; for the eunuch, being clever by nature, understood that she was in love. "Oh," he said, "most foolish of all women, do you prefer the slave of Mithridates to the King?" Callirhoe was indignant at Chaereas being insulted, and said: "Speak no ill, man.
7.10. Chaereas is well-born, of a leading city, which not even the Athenians defeated — those who at Marathon and Salamis defeated your Great King." As she said this she let fall springs of tears; but the eunuch pressed her the harder and said: "You are the cause of your own delay.
7.11. How, then, will you have the judge favourable, so as to recover your husband too? Perhaps Chaereas would not even learn what had been done; but even if he learned it, he would not be jealous of his superior;
7.12. rather he would think you the more honoured, as having pleased the King." He added this not for her sake but because he himself thought so; for all the barbarians are awestruck and reckon the King a manifest god. But Callirhoe would not have welcomed marriage even with Zeus himself, nor would she have preferred immortality to a single day with Chaereas.
7.13. So the eunuch, able to accomplish nothing, said: "I grant you, woman, time for reflection. But consider not about yourself alone, but also about Chaereas, who is in danger of perishing by the most piteous death; for the King will not endure to be outdone in love." And with that he departed; but this last word of the conversation struck Callirhoe.
8.1. But Fortune quickly changed all reflection and all amorous converse, finding occasion for newer events; for messengers came to the King reporting that Egypt had revolted with a great force.
8.2. The Egyptians had killed the King's satrap, had chosen a king from among the natives, and he, setting out from Memphis, had crossed Pelusium and was already overrunning Syria and Phoenicia, so that the cities could no longer hold out, as though some torrent or fire had suddenly poured over them.
8.3. At the report the King was troubled, and the Persians were dismayed; and dejection seized all Babylon. Then too the King's interpreters of dreams and the seers declared that they had foretold what was coming; for the gods, in demanding sacrifices, were signifying danger, but also victory.
8.4. All the things that usually happen, and all that is to be expected in an unforeseen war, were both said and came to pass; for a great commotion seized Asia. So the King, summoning the Persian peers and as many leaders of the nations as were present — those with whom he was accustomed to transact great matters — took counsel about the situation, and one advised one thing and another another.

title: Callirhoe
text:
8.5. But it pleased all to make haste and not to delay even a single day if possible, for two reasons: both to check the enemy from growing greater, and to make their friends more cheerful by showing them help close at hand. If they delayed, everything would turn out the opposite way: the enemy would grow contemptuous, as of men afraid, and their own people would give way, as of men neglected.
8.6. And it was the greatest good fortune for the King that he had been caught not in Bactra, nor in Ecbatana, but in Babylon, near Syria; for once he had crossed the Euphrates he would have the rebels at once in his hands. So it was resolved to lead out the force already about him, and to send everywhere orders for the army to gather at the river Euphrates. The mustering of the force is very easy for the Persians.
8.7. For it has been ordained by Cyrus, the first to reign over the Persians, which of the nations must furnish cavalry for war and how many in number, which infantry and how many, which archers, and how many chariots each — both unarmed and scythe-bearing — and elephants from where and how many, and money from whom and how much. And all is made ready by all in just so much time as a single man takes to make ready.
9.1. On the fifth day after the news the King marched out of Babylon, with everyone of military age following him by a general command. Among these Dionysius too went out; for he was an Ionian, and none of the subjects was permitted to remain.
9.2. Adorning himself with the finest armour, and forming a not contemptible company from those about him, he placed himself among the foremost and most conspicuous, and was plainly going to do something noble, as a man naturally ambitious and one who did not count valour a secondary thing,
9.3. but held himself worthy of the noblest deeds. And then he had a light hope as well, that if he proved useful in the war he would receive from the King, even without trial, the woman as the prize of his valour.
9.4. As for Callirhoe, the queen did not wish to take her along; for this reason she did not even mention her to the King, nor ask what he commanded to be done about the foreigner. And Artaxates too kept silent, ostensibly not daring, while his master was in danger, to make mention of an amorous diversion, but in truth glad to be rid of her as of a wild beast; he seemed all but to feel gratitude to the war for cutting short the King's desire, which had been nourished by idleness.
9.5. Yet the King had not forgotten Callirhoe; rather, in that indescribable confusion a certain memory of her beauty came over him. But he was ashamed to say anything about her, lest he should seem altogether childish, making mention of a beautiful woman in so great a war. As his impulse pressed him, he said nothing to Statira herself, nor even to the eunuch, since he knew that the eunuch was aware of his love; but he devised something of this kind.
9.6. It is the custom for the King himself and for the noblest of the Persians, when they go out to war, to take along their wives and children and gold and silver and clothing and eunuchs and concubines and dogs and tables and costly wealth and luxury.
9.7. So calling the steward in charge of these things, the King, after first saying much and arranging all the rest as each thing was to be done, mentioned Callirhoe last, with a face of credible indifference, as though she did not concern him at all. "And let that foreign woman too," he said, "about whom I undertook the trial, follow along with the other women."

title: Callirhoe
text:
9.8. And so Callirhoe left Babylon not unwillingly, for she hoped that Chaereas too would go out; and that war brings much that is uncertain, and changes for the better to those in misfortune; and that perhaps the trial too would reach its end there, once a swift peace had come about.
1.1. While everyone was marching out with the King to the war against the Egyptians, no one gave any order to Chaereas; for he was not the King's slave, but was then the only free man in Babylon. And he rejoiced, hoping that Callirhoe would remain. So the next day he came to the palace, looking for the woman.
1.2. Seeing it shut up and many guards at the doors, he went round the whole city searching, and continually, like a madman, kept asking his friend Polycharmus: "Where is Callirhoe? What has become of her? Surely she too is not on campaign?"
1.3. Not finding Callirhoe, he looked for Dionysius his rival, and came to his house. Then someone came forward as though by chance and said what he had been taught to say. For Dionysius, wishing to make Chaereas despair of the marriage with Callirhoe and no longer wait for the trial, had devised something of this kind.
1.4. Going out to the battle, he had left behind a man to report to Chaereas that the King of the Persians, having need of allies, had sent Dionysius to gather an army against the Egyptian, and, so that he might serve him faithfully and zealously, had given Callirhoe back to him. On hearing this, Chaereas believed it at once; for a man in misfortune is easily deceived.
1.5. So tearing his clothes and rending his hair, beating his breast at the same time, he said: "Faithless Babylon, evil host, deserted in my case as well! O fine judge — he has become the procurer of another man's wife! A wedding in time of war! And I was rehearsing my case and was fully persuaded that I would plead justly; but I have been condemned by default, and Dionysius has won by saying nothing.
1.6. But his victory will profit him nothing; for Callirhoe will not live, parted from Chaereas while he is present, and at the first it was the belief that I was dead that deceived her. Why then do I delay, and not cut my own throat before the palace, pouring out my blood on the doors of the judge? Let Persians and Medes know how the King gave judgment here."
1.7. But Polycharmus, seeing that his friend's calamity was inconsolable and that Chaereas could not be saved, said: "Long ago, dearest friend, I used to console you, and often kept you from dying; but now you seem to me to have resolved well. So far am I from hindering you that I myself am now ready to die with you. But let us consider what manner of death would be better; for the one you intend brings some odium upon the King and shame for the future, but no great revenge for what we have suffered.
1.8. It seems to me that we should use the death we have once resolved on to take vengeance on the tyrant. For it is a fine thing, having grieved him by some deed, to make him repent, leaving to those who come after a noble tale, that two Greeks who had been wronged repaid the Great King with grief and died like men."
1.9. "How, then," said Chaereas, "can we, alone and poor and foreigners, grieve the master of so many great nations, who has such power as we have seen? For there are guards and outguards about his person; and even if we kill someone of his, even if we burn some of his possessions, he will not feel the loss."
1.10. "You would be right to say this," said Polycharmus, "were it not for the war; but as it is, we hear that Egypt has revolted, that Phoenicia has been captured, that Syria is being overrun. War will meet the King even before he crosses the Euphrates.

title: Callirhoe
text:
1.11. So we are not the only two; rather we have as many allies as the Egyptian leads — so many arms, so much money, so many triremes. Let us use another's strength for our own revenge." Not yet was the whole word spoken when Chaereas cried out: "Let us hasten, let us be off! I will take justice on the judge in the war."
2.1. So setting out quickly, they pursued the King, pretending to wish to campaign with him; for by this pretext they hoped to cross the Euphrates without fear. They overtook the army at the river and, joining the rear-guard, followed along.
2.2. When they came to Syria, they deserted to the Egyptian, and the guards, seizing them, examined who they were; for, not having the bearing of envoys, they were rather suspected of being spies. There too they were in danger, had not a certain Greek, found there by chance, understood their speech. They asked to be led to the king, as bringing him a great benefit.
2.3. When they had been brought, Chaereas said: "We are Greeks, Syracusans of noble birth. This man came to Babylon, being my friend, for my sake, and I for the sake of a woman, the daughter of Hermocrates — if you have heard of any Hermocrates, a general who defeated the Athenians at sea." The Egyptian nodded;
2.4. for no nation was ignorant of the misfortune of the Athenians, which they suffered in the Sicilian war. "Artaxerxes has tyrannized over us," and he related everything. "So bringing ourselves, we give ourselves to you as faithful friends, having the two most powerful incitements to courage — a love of death and of revenge. For already I am dead, so far as concerns my misfortunes; what remains, I live only to grieve my enemy. 'May I not die without a struggle and without glory, but having done some great thing for men yet to come to hear of.'"
2.5. Hearing this, the Egyptian was pleased, and taking his right hand said: "You have come in good time, young man, both for yourself and for me." At once, then, he ordered arms and a tent to be given them, and not long after he made Chaereas his table-companion, and then his counsellor; for Chaereas showed prudence and courage, and with these also faithfulness, as one not unprovided with a good nature and education.
2.6. His rivalry with the King roused him the more and made him more distinguished, and his wish to show that he was not contemptible but worthy of honour. So at once he displayed a great deed. To the Egyptian everything else had gone forward easily, and he had become master of Coele-Syria at a single stroke; Phoenicia too was subject to him, except for Tyre.
2.7. But the Tyrians are by nature a most warlike people, and wish to possess glory for courage, lest they seem to disgrace Heracles, the most manifest god among them, to whom alone they have practically dedicated the city. They take confidence also in the strength of their dwelling-place.
2.8. For the city is settled in the sea, and a narrow entrance joining it to the land keeps it from being an island; it is like a ship at anchor, having put its gangway down upon the land.
2.9. So it is easy for them to shut out war on every side: the land army by the sea, since a single gate suffices against it, and the sailing-up of the triremes by walls, the city being strongly built and closed off by harbours like a house.
3.1. So when all the surrounding country had been taken, the Tyrians alone despised the Egyptians, keeping their goodwill and faith to the Persian. Vexed at this, the Egyptian gathered a council. Then for the first time he summoned Chaereas to the deliberation, and spoke thus: "Men, my allies —

title: Callirhoe
text:
3.2. for I would not call my friends slaves — you see the difficulty: that, like a ship that has sailed prosperously for a long way, we are caught by a contrary wind, and most troublesome Tyre holds us back when we are pressing on. The King too is hastening, as we learn. What, then, must we do? For it is not possible either to take Tyre or to pass it by; rather, lying like a wall in the midst, it shuts off all Asia from us. It seems to me that we should leave here as quickly as possible, before the Persian force is added to the Tyrians.
3.3. There is danger in our being caught in enemy country. But Pelusium is a stronghold, where we fear neither Tyrians nor Medes nor all mankind coming against us; for there is impassable sand and a narrow entrance, and the sea is ours, and the Nile loves the Egyptians." When he had said this very cautiously, there was silence among all, and dejection; but Chaereas alone dared to speak: "O King —
3.4. for you are truly a king, not the Persian, the basest of men — you have grieved me by deliberating about flight in the hour of victory; for we are winning, if the gods will, and we shall hold not only Tyre but Babylon too. Many obstacles arise in war, before which one must not utterly shrink back, but set one's hand to the work, always putting forward good hope.
3.5. These Tyrians, who now mock us, I will set before you stripped and in fetters. If you do not believe it, sacrifice me first and depart; for while I live I will not share in flight. But if you wish it at all costs, leave me a few who will willingly remain; and 'we two, Polycharmus and I, will fight; for we have come with a god.'"
3.6. All were ashamed not to assent to Chaereas's opinion; and the King, marvelling at his spirit, granted him to take as many of the picked army as he wished. But he did not choose them at once; rather, mingling himself into the camp, and ordering Polycharmus to do the same, he first searched out whether there were any Greeks in the camp.
3.7. Many of the mercenaries were found, and he chose Lacedaemonians and Corinthians and the other Peloponnesians; he found also about twenty Sicilians. So having made up three hundred in number, he spoke thus: "Men of Greece,
3.8. since the King gave me leave to pick the best of the army, I chose you; for I myself am a Greek, a Syracusan by descent. And you must surpass the rest not only in nobility of birth but also in valour.
3.9. Let no one, then, be dismayed at the deed to which I summon you; for we shall find it possible and easy — difficult in appearance rather than in experience. So few Greeks withstood Xerxes at Thermopylae. The Tyrians are not five million, but a few, and they use contempt with arrogance, not spirit with good counsel.
3.10. Let them learn, then, how much Greeks surpass Phoenicians. As for me, I do not desire command, but am ready to follow whoever of you wishes to lead; for he will find me obedient, since I aim not at my own glory but at the common one." All shouted: "Be our general, with our consent." He said: "I am your general, and you yourselves have given me the command;
3.11. for this reason I will try to do everything so that you may not repent having chosen goodwill and faith toward me. But for the present, with the gods' help, you will become glorious and conspicuous and the richest of the allies, and for the future you will leave behind an immortal name of valour; and all men, as they celebrate the three hundred with Othryadas or those with Leonidas, so will celebrate those with Chaereas." While he was still speaking, all cried out, "Lead on!" and all rushed to their arms.

title: Callirhoe
text:
4.1. Adorning them with the finest panoplies, Chaereas led them to the King's tent. Seeing them, the Egyptian marvelled and supposed he was looking at others, not his usual men, and he promised them great gifts.
4.2. "These," said Chaereas, "we take on trust; but do you keep the rest of the army under arms, and do not advance against Tyre before we have mastered it and, having mounted the walls, call you."
4.3. "May the gods grant it so," he said. So Chaereas led those men, packed close together, against Tyre, so that they seemed far fewer; and truly: "shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man." And at first they were not even observed by the enemy; but when they were near, those on the walls, seeing them, signalled to those within, expecting anything rather than that they were enemies.
4.4. For who would have expected that men so few would come against the mightiest of cities, against which not even the whole force of the Egyptians had ever dared to come? When they drew near the walls, they asked who they were and what they wanted.
4.5. Chaereas answered: "We are Greek mercenaries, not receiving our pay from the Egyptian, but even plotted against to our destruction; we have come to you, wishing to take vengeance with you upon the common enemy."
4.6. Someone reported this to those within, and the general, opening the gates, came forward with a few. Chaereas, killing him first, rushed upon the rest, "and he smote them turning this way and that, and an unseemly groaning arose from them." One killed another, like lions falling upon an unguarded herd of cattle; and wailing and lamentation held the whole city, few seeing what was happening, but all in confusion.
4.7. And a disordered crowd poured out through the gate, wishing to see what had befallen. This above all destroyed the Tyrians.
4.8. For those within forced their way out, while those outside, struck and pierced with swords and spears, fled back within; and meeting one another in the narrow space, they gave great opportunity to the killers. Nor was it even possible to shut the gates, the dead being heaped up in them.
4.9. In this indescribable confusion Chaereas alone kept his head; for forcing his way through those who met him and getting inside the gates, he leapt up onto the walls, himself the tenth man, and from above signalled, calling the Egyptians, who came faster than word, and Tyre was taken.
4.10. When Tyre had been taken, all the others held festival, but Chaereas alone neither sacrificed nor crowned himself. "For what profit have I in a victory celebration, if you, Callirhoe, do not see it? I will no longer wear a garland since that wedding night. For whether you are dead, I do wrong; or whether you live, how can I hold festival without you, while you are perhaps lying in such straits?"
4.11. But the King of the Persians, having crossed the Euphrates, hastened to engage the enemy as quickly as possible. For learning that Tyre had been taken, he feared for Sidon and for all Syria, seeing his enemy already a match for him.
4.12. For this reason he resolved no longer to travel with all his retinue, but more lightly equipped, so that nothing might hinder his speed. Taking the purest part of the army, he left behind there, with the queen, the useless ages, and the money and the clothing and the royal treasure.
4.13. But since everything was full of tumult and disturbance, and the war had seized the cities as far as the Euphrates, it seemed safer to deposit those left behind on Aradus.

title: Callirhoe
text:
5.1. This is an island, distant thirty stades from the mainland, having an ancient temple of Aphrodite. So as if in a house, the women passed their time there with complete security.
5.2. When Callirhoe beheld the Aphrodite, standing opposite her she at first was silent and wept, reproaching the goddess with her tears; at last she murmured: "See, here too is Aradus, a little island instead of great Sicily, and no one of mine here.
5.3. It is enough, mistress. How long will you war against me? If indeed I have offended you at all, you have punished me; if even my unlucky beauty seemed to you a thing to envy, it has become to me the cause of ruin. The one thing that was wanting to my misfortunes — I have now tasted war as well.
5.4. Compared with my present plight, even Babylon was kind to me. There Chaereas was near. But now surely he is dead; for when I went away he would not have lived. Yet I have no one from whom I can learn what has become of him.
5.5. All are strangers, all barbarians, envious, hating; and worse than those who hate are those who love. Do you, mistress, show me whether Chaereas lives." While she was still saying this, Rhodogune came up — daughter of Zopyrus, wife of Megabyzus, both her father and her husband among the noblest of the Persians; this was the woman who had first of the Persian ladies met Callirhoe when she entered Babylon.
5.6. The Egyptian, when he heard that the King was near and prepared both by land and by sea, calling Chaereas, said: "I have not had the chance to repay the first of your successes; for you gave me Tyre. But concerning what follows I beg you, let us not lose the blessings already in our hands, in which I will make you a partner.
5.7. For Egypt suffices me, but Syria shall become a possession for you. Come then, let us consider what is to be done; for the war is at its height in both elements. To you I entrust the choice, whether you wish to command the land or the naval force.
5.8. I think the sea is more proper to you; for you Syracusans defeated the Athenians too at sea. Today your contest is against the Persians, who were defeated by the Athenians. You have Egyptian triremes, larger and more numerous than the Sicilian; imitate your kinsman Hermocrates on the sea." Chaereas answered: "Every danger is sweet to me; on your behalf I will take up the war, even against the King who is most hostile to me.
5.9. Give me, along with the triremes, my own three hundred as well." "Take these," he said, "and others, as many as you wish." And at once the word became a deed; for need pressed. The Egyptian, with the land army, went to meet the enemy,
5.10. while Chaereas was appointed admiral. This made the infantry more dispirited, because Chaereas was not campaigning with them; for they already loved him and had good hopes when he was general. It seemed as though an eye had been torn from a great body.
5.11. But the naval force was lifted up by hope and filled with spirit, because they had the bravest and fairest man as their leader. They mourned little or not at all, but the trierarchs and pilots and sailors and soldiers all alike were eager — each to be the first to display his zeal to Chaereas.
5.12. On the same day the battle was joined both by land and by sea. For a long time the land army of the Egyptians held out against the Medes and Persians, then, overborne by numbers, they gave way. And the King, mounted, pursued. The Egyptian was eager to take refuge in Pelusium, and the Persian to overtake him sooner; and perhaps he would even have escaped, had not Dionysius displayed a marvellous deed.

title: Callirhoe
text:
5.13. In the engagement he fought brilliantly, always fighting near the King so that he might see him, and was the first to rout those opposite him. And then, when the flight was long and continuous by day and by night, seeing the King grieved at this, he said: "Do not grieve, master; for I will keep the Egyptian from escaping, if you give me picked horsemen." The King praised him and gave them;
5.14. and he, taking five thousand, covered two stages in one day, and falling upon the Egyptians at night, unexpected, he took many alive and killed still more. The Egyptian, caught alive, cut his own throat, and Dionysius brought his head to the King.
5.15. When the King saw it, he said: "I will enroll you as a benefactor of my house, and even now I give you the most welcome gift, the one you yourself most of all desire — Callirhoe. The war has decided the case. You have the fairest prize of valour." Dionysius did homage and thought himself the equal of a god, persuaded that he was now securely the husband of Callirhoe.
6.1. These things were happening on land; but on the sea Chaereas conquered, so that the enemy fleet was no match for him; for they did not receive the charges of the Egyptian triremes, nor took up a prow-to-prow stand at all, but some were at once overturned, and others, driven ashore, he captured crews and all; and the sea was filled with Median wreckage.
6.2. But neither did the King know of the defeat of his own men at sea, nor Chaereas of that of the Egyptians on land; each thought himself victorious in both. So on that day on which he had fought at sea, Chaereas, sailing in to Aradus, ordered men to sail round the island in a circle and keep guard, intending to render account of it to his master.
6.3. And they gathered the eunuchs and maidservants and all the cheaper sort of persons into the market-place, for it had open space. So great was the multitude that they passed the night not only in the colonnades but also in the open air.
6.4. Those of some rank they brought into a building of the market-place, in which the magistrates were accustomed to transact business. The women sat on the ground around the queen, and they neither kindled a fire nor tasted food; for they had learned that the King had been captured and that the Persian cause was lost, and that the Egyptian was everywhere victorious.
6.5. That night was both the sweetest and the most grievous that held Aradus. For the Egyptians rejoiced at being freed from war and from Persian slavery, while the captured Persians expected chains and whips and outrages and slaughter, and, as the most merciful thing, slavery. Statira, laying her head on Callirhoe's knees, wept; and Callirhoe, as a Greek and an educated woman, not unpractised in misfortunes, did most to console the queen.
6.6. And something of this kind happened. An Egyptian soldier, who had been entrusted with guarding those in the building, learning that the queen was within, did not dare to approach near her — according to the innate reverence of the barbarians for the royal name — but standing by the closed door,
6.7. he said: "Take heart, mistress; for now the admiral does not know that you too have been shut up here with the captives, but when he learns it he will provide for you kindly. For he is not only brave but will also make you his wife; for by nature he is a lover of women." On hearing this, Callirhoe wailed aloud and tore her hair, saying: "Now in truth I am a captive. Kill me rather than announce such things.

title: Callirhoe
text:
6.8. Marriage I will not endure; death I pray for. Let them pierce and burn me, from here I will not rise; this place shall be my tomb. But if, as you say, the general is humane, let him grant me this favour:
6.9. let him kill me here." That man brought his entreaties to her again, but she would not rise; rather, veiling herself, she fell to the ground and lay there. Deliberation lay before the Egyptian as to what he should do; for he did not dare to use force, but again he could not persuade her. Therefore, turning back, he came to Chaereas with a downcast face.
6.10. Seeing him, Chaereas said: "This is another matter. Some men are stealing the fairest of the spoils, but they will not do it and rejoice." When the Egyptian said: "No harm has come to any woman, master; for the woman whom I found set among the broad ranks does not wish to come, but has flung herself on the ground, asking for a sword and wishing to die," Chaereas laughed and said: "O most witless of all men, do you not know how a woman is won over by entreaties, praises, promises, and most of all if she thinks herself loved? But you, perhaps, used force and insult." "No, master;
6.11. but all these things you speak of I did, twice over the more. For I even lied to you that you would have her as your wife,
6.12. and at this above all she was indignant." Chaereas said: "Charming, then, I must be, and lovable, if even before seeing me she turned away from me and hated me! It seems the woman has a spirit not ignoble. Let no one use force on her, but let her live as she has chosen; for it befits me to honour chastity. And she too, perhaps, is mourning a husband."
1.1. How Chaereas, suspecting that Callirhoe had been handed over to Dionysius, and wishing to take vengeance on the King, deserted to the Egyptian, and being appointed admiral mastered the sea, and, victorious, took Aradus, where the King had deposited his own wife and all his retinue and Callirhoe —
1.2. all this has been set out in the previous book. But Fortune was about to do something not only strange but also grievous: that Chaereas, while he had Callirhoe, should not know it, and, taking up the women of others, should carry them off in his triremes, but leave his own alone there — not, like Ariadne, sleeping, nor for Dionysus as her bridegroom, but as spoil for his own enemies.
1.3. But this seemed dreadful to Aphrodite. For by now she was being reconciled to him, having before been bitterly angry at his untimely jealousy, because, when he had received from her the fairest gift — such as not even Alexander, that is, Paris — he had outraged her favour. But since Chaereas had made a good defence to Love, having wandered from west to east through a thousand sufferings, Aphrodite took pity on him; and the pair of the two fairest, which she had joined together from the beginning, having exercised them by land and sea, she wished now to restore.
1.4. And I think that this last book too will prove the most pleasant to those who read it; for it is a purgation of the grievous things in the earlier ones. No longer is there piracy and slavery and trial and battle and self-starvation and war and capture, but lawful loves now and legitimate marriages.
1.5. How, then, the goddess brought the truth to light and showed to each other those who did not know each other, I will tell.
It was evening, and many of the captives were still left behind. So Chaereas, weary, rose
1.6. to give orders for the voyage. As he was passing through the market-place, the Egyptian said to him: "Here is the woman, master, who refuses to come forward but is starving herself. Perhaps you will persuade her to rise; for why must you leave behind the fairest of the spoils?" Polycharmus too joined in the suggestion, wishing to throw him, if somehow he could, into a new love and a consolation for Callirhoe. "Let us go in,"

title: Callirhoe
text:
1.7. he said, "Chaereas." So crossing the threshold, and seeing her flung down and veiled, at once from her breathing and her posture his soul was troubled, and he became excited; indeed he would surely have recognized her, had he not been so firmly persuaded that Dionysius had recovered Callirhoe.
1.8. Approaching gently, he said: "Take heart, woman, whoever you are; for we will not force you, but you shall have the husband you wish." While he was still speaking, Callirhoe, recognizing the voice, unveiled herself, and both cried out together, "Chaereas!" "Callirhoe!" and, throwing their arms about each other,
1.9. they swooned and fell. Polycharmus too at first stood speechless at the marvel, but as time went on he said: "Rise, you have recovered each other; the gods have fulfilled the prayers of you both. But remember that you are not in your homeland, but in an enemy land, and you must first manage these matters well,
1.10. so that no one may part you again." Such things he shouted at them; and they, like people who have been plunged in a deep well and have barely heard a voice from above, slowly came up; then, seeing each other and kissing, they sank down again, and a second and a third time they did the same,
uttering one cry: "I have you, if you are truly Callirhoe — if you are truly Chaereas."
1.11. A rumour ran round that the admiral had found his wife. No soldier stayed in his tent, no sailor in his trireme, no doorkeeper in his house; from every side they came running, saying: "O blessed woman, she has won the most beautiful of husbands!" But when Callirhoe appeared, no one any longer praised Chaereas, but all looked upon her, as though she alone existed.
1.12. She walked in stately fashion, with Chaereas and Polycharmus escorting her in their midst. Flowers and garlands were thrown over them, and wine and perfume were poured before their feet; and there were together the sweetest things of war and of peace, a victory celebration and a wedding.
1.13. Now Chaereas was accustomed to sleep in his trireme, busy with many things both by night and by day; but then, entrusting everything to Polycharmus, he himself did not even wait for night, but went into the royal chamber; for in each city a special house is set apart for the Great King.
1.14. A couch of beaten gold stood there, with bedding of Tyrian purple, the weaving Babylonian. Who could describe that night, how full it was of stories, how full of tears together and kisses? First Callirhoe began to relate how she had come back to life in the tomb, how she had been carried off by Theron, how she had sailed, how she had been sold.
1.15. Up to this point Chaereas wept as he listened; but when the story came to Miletus, Callirhoe fell silent in shame, and Chaereas remembered his innate jealousy, but the account of the child consoled him. Before hearing it all, he said: "Tell me how you came to Aradus, and where you left Dionysius, and what you did about the King."
1.16. And she at once swore that she had not seen Dionysius since the trial, and that the King loved her, but that she had not had intercourse with him, not even to a kiss. "Then I was unjust," said Chaereas, "and quick to anger, having done such dreadful things to the King when he was doing you no wrong; for, parted from you, I was driven to the necessity of desertion.
1.17. But I did not bring shame upon you; I have filled land and sea with trophies." And he related everything exactly, glorying in his achievements. When there had been enough of tears and tales, embracing each other, "gladly they came to the rite of their old bed."

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.1. While it was still night, a certain Egyptian, not of the obscure, sailed in, and stepping from his cutter, asked in haste where Chaereas was. Led, then, to Polycharmus, he said that he could tell the secret to no one else, and that the need on which he had come was pressing.
2.2. For a long time Polycharmus put off the entry to Chaereas, not wishing to disturb him at an unseasonable hour; but since the man pressed, opening the chamber door a little, he disclosed the urgency. And Chaereas, like a good general, said: "Call him in; for war does not wait for delay." So the Egyptian was brought in,
2.3. while it was still dark, and standing by the couch said: "Know that the King of the Persians has killed the Egyptian, and has sent part of the army to Egypt to settle affairs there, and is leading all the rest here, and will be present any moment now; for having learned that Aradus has been taken, he grieves both for all the wealth he left here, and most of all is in anguish about Statira his wife."
2.4. Hearing this, Chaereas sprang up; but Callirhoe, taking hold of him, said: "Where do you rush before deliberating about what is at hand? For if you make this public, you will stir up a great war for yourself, since all already know and despise us; and falling again into their hands we shall suffer things heavier than before."
2.5. Quickly he was persuaded by her counsel, and came out of the chamber with craft. For holding the Egyptian by the hand, and calling the multitude together, he said: "We are victorious, men, over the land army of the King too; for this man brings us the good news and letters from the Egyptian; and we must sail as quickly as possible to where he ordered. So pack up, all of you, and embark."
2.6. When he had said this, the trumpeter sounded the signal of recall to the triremes. The spoils and captives they had stowed on board the day before, and nothing was left on the island except what was heavy and useless.
2.7. Then they loosed the moorings and weighed anchor, and the harbour was filled with shouting and confusion, and each man busied himself with something. As Chaereas was passing to the triremes, he gave a secret command to the trierarchs to sail for Cyprus, on the ground that it was necessary to seize it first while it was still unguarded; and using a favouring wind, on the next day they put in at Paphos, where there is a temple of Aphrodite.
2.8. When they had anchored, Chaereas, before anyone disembarked from the triremes, first sent out heralds to proclaim peace and a truce to the inhabitants. When they had received him, he landed his whole force and honoured Aphrodite with offerings; and many victims being collected, he feasted the army.
2.9. As he was considering what was to come next, the priests — who are also seers — reported that the victims had been favourable. Then, taking courage, he called the trierarchs and the three hundred Greeks and as many of the Egyptians as he saw well-disposed toward him, and spoke thus: "Fellow soldiers and friends,
2.10. partners in great achievements, to me both the fairest peace and the safest war is with you; for by experience we have learned that, being of one mind, we mastered the sea. But a critical moment is upon us, for deliberating about future safety; for you know that the Egyptian has been killed in battle, and the King rules all the land, while we have been cut off in the midst of the enemy.
2.11. Does anyone, then, advise us to go off to the King and, carrying ourselves, throw ourselves into his hands?" They cried out at once that anything rather than this must be done. "Where, then, shall we go? For everything is hostile to us, and we can no longer even trust the sea, since the land is mastered by the enemy; for surely we cannot fly away."

title: Callirhoe
text:
2.12.
